facts: Sheepskin boots Australian surfers wore to warm up after sessions; Brian Smith started selling them in California in 1978.
Deckers Outdoor bought the brand in 1995 and holds 'UGG' as a trademark in the US and elsewhere; in Australia, 'ugg' is a generic word any bootmaker may use.
In 2019, a US jury found an Australian maker liable for selling boots labelled 'ugg' into the United States.
Oprah Winfrey featured them in her 'Favorite Things' lists repeatedly in the 2000s, which drove the first boom.
UGG is Deckers' largest brand, with over $2 billion in annual sales.

a.text: UGG boots. The only footwear named after a review. Australian surfers made these to warm their feet after the ocean, and somehow America decided the ocean was the mall. They're sheepskin, which means a sheep died so you could wear a slipper to the DMV. One puddle and they're covered in salt lines like a topographic map of everywhere you regret going. Zero arch support, so after two weeks your heel caves sideways and you're walking on the boot's ankle like it owes you money. You wear them barefoot, so by February they smell like a wet lamb's final wish. They're as waterproof as a muffin. Oprah put them on her Favorite Things list. She's since moved on. Twenty years later they're back with platform soles, proving even a mistake wants to be taller.

b.text: Let's hear it for the people wearing UGGs in July. You're not dressing for the weather. You're dressing for 2005, still waiting for Paris Hilton to text back. Australian surfers made these to warm their feet after the ocean. You wear them to warm your feet after the Trader Joe's parking lot. In August. In Phoenix. What are you after? "Comfort," you say. Babe, your ankles have been collapsing outward since the Bush administration. You walk like a Clydesdale that's given up. And what does it get you? One summer rainstorm and you're squelching through Target like a wet golden retriever who made bad choices. People don't ask where you got them. They ask if you're okay. Congratulations: you've turned footwear into a wellness check.

Word has been around for forty years and still can't decide what font it is. Times New Roman, then Calibri, now Aptos. It's having a midlife crisis in 11-point.

It underlines my own name in red. Wavy red. Like *I'm* the typo.

Try making a numbered list. Word says, "Got it, starting at 1." Second item: "Also 1." Third item: "Here's 4. It's indented. It's a letter now."

And Track Changes isn't a feature. It's a crime scene: strikethroughs everywhere, plus forty comments from someone named "Author."

Word, you gave us Clippy, and somehow he was the most helpful part.

b.text: You chose Word for your thesis because you "didn't have time to learn LaTeX." Beautiful. Instead you learned section breaks, by force, at 3 a.m., trying to make page numbers switch from Roman to Arabic without page one of Chapter 2 becoming page xvii. You wanted to spend your time on research. Instead you spend it dragging a figure half an inch and watching four chapters collapse like a Jenga tower built by your enemies. Your committee will open the PDF and see "Error! Reference source not found." in the middle of your key finding, which, honestly, is a fair summary of your methodology. Your folder contains thesis_FINAL_v9_REALfinal_USE_THIS.docx, because you are a scientist who trusts nothing except filenames. Five years of work, and your proudest skill is knowing which heading style secretly isn't Heading 2.

facts: Founded in Boulder, Colorado, in 2002; the first clog debuted at the Fort Lauderdale boat show as a boating shoe.
Made of 'Croslite', which Crocs describes as a proprietary closed-cell resin foam and which third parties identify as an injection-moulded EVA foam.
Balenciaga sold a platform Crocs for about $850 in 2018.
The stock fell more than 90% from its 2007 peak during the 2008 crisis; the company then boomed in the pandemic and gave away 860,000 pairs to healthcare workers in 2020.
The holes are officially 'ventilation ports' and the charms that go in them are 'Jibbitz', a company Crocs bought in 2006.

a.text: People who wear Crocs in public want you to know they've stopped trying, but they also want credit for it. That's why they buy the Jibbitz. Nothing says "I don't care what you think" like spending forty dollars on tiny rubber tacos so everyone knows exactly what you think. Then there's the strap. You flipped it back into "Sport Mode," which is a bold claim from a man walking into Applebee's. Your nurse friend wears them because she stands for twelve-hour shifts. You wear them for a twelve-minute Target run, hoping to borrow a little of her dignity. And what does it get you? Comfort, sure. Plus a lifetime of strangers asking if you're coming off a shift. You're not, Kyle. You're coming off a nap.

b.text:
Crocs. The only shoe that looks like a colander that wanted to go to brunch. Thirteen holes, and somehow none of them let the dignity out, because there was never any in there.

You were invented as a boat shoe. A *boat* shoe. The one place you were built for, and you'd just float away. So you stayed on land and started fights with escalators. Malls had to post warnings. You're the only footwear with a rap sheet against machinery.

And "sport mode"? Flipping a strap behind your heel doesn't make you athletic. It makes you a clog wearing a seatbelt.

Then came Jibbitz, little charms you jam into the holes so grown adults can accessorize ventilation. Congratulations. You turned a shoe into a fridge door.

facts: Invented in 1957 by Albert Lamorisse, the French director of The Red Balloon, as La Conquête du Monde; Parker Brothers published it in the United States in 1959.
The map has 42 territories, among them Kamchatka, Irkutsk, and Yakutsk, while the entire Middle East is one territory.
Holding Australia, which has a single entry point, is the standard opening strategy.
A full game can run for hours, and players eliminated early have nothing to do but watch.

a.text: You people who play Risk to the end are a special breed. Six hours in, Dad's still holed up in Australia like it's a tax shelter, your cousin is defending Kamchatka like he was born there, and nobody remembers why we hate Steve, only that we do. You're not after world domination. You're after the exact moment your sister breaks the nonaggression pact in Ukraine, so you can bring it up at Thanksgiving for eleven years. And what does winning get you? A board covered entirely in your color, a table of people who no longer speak to you, and the hollow joy of conquering Earth with the luck of a man who only rolls double sixes when defending Irkutsk. Congratulations, Napoleon. It's 2 a.m. The pizza's cold. Your empire goes back in the box.

b.text:
Risk is the only game where you can conquer the entire planet and still lose to the guy who's been hiding in Australia since 7 p.m. Four territories, one entrance, and he just sits there like a guy at a party who won't leave the snack table.

This game has a map drawn by someone who heard about geography once, at a bar. Kamchatka borders Alaska. Ukraine is the size of Brazil. Yakutsk and Irkutsk are vital military objectives, and nobody at the table can find them on a real map.

The rules say the defender wins ties, which is the most realistic thing about it, because nobody actually finishes Risk. They just quit at 2 a.m. when someone's dad flips the board over Siberia.

And the pieces? Little plastic cannons and horses. Napoleonic warfare, global scale, and the whole thing is decided by rolling a 6 against your cousin Greg.

facts: First shipped for the Macintosh in 1985; the Windows version followed in 1987.

Silently converts gene names such as SEPT2 and MARCH1 into dates; by August 2020 the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee had renamed 27 human genes (MARCH1 became MARCHF1, SEPT2 became SEPTIN2) and published guidelines in Nature Genetics to stop it.
In October 2020, Public Health England lost 15,841 COVID-19 cases when a legacy .xls file hit its 65,536-row limit.
Reinhart and Rogoff's 2010 paper 'Growth in a Time of Debt', cited for austerity policies, omitted five countries through a spreadsheet range error found by a graduate student in 2013.
Sheets have been capped at 1,048,576 rows by 16,384 columns since Excel 2007.

a.text: You people run a forty-million-dollar company out of a file called Budget_FINAL_v9_USE_THIS_ONE.xlsx. You don't want software. You want power: specifically, being the only person alive who knows why cell AF212 is hardcoded to 7. Your entire supply chain hangs on a VLOOKUP Gary wrote in 2011, and Gary is dead. Well, he's in Boise. Same thing. You call it "agile." Your auditors call it "a crime scene with conditional formatting." Every quarter-end the file says "locked for editing by Brenda," and the whole company just waits for Brenda. And when you finally hit row 1,048,576, did you buy a database? No. You started Sheet2. That's not a business. That's a hostage situation with freeze panes.

b.text:
Excel, you're the only software so powerful that scientists had to rename human genes because you kept turning MARCH1 into a date. You didn't adapt to biology; biology adapted to you. Type a phone number and you lop off the leading zero like it owes you money. Enter a credit card number and you serve back 4.53E+15, as if I'm splitting dinner with a physicist.

You still think 1900 was a leap year. It wasn't. You've known for decades. You just don't care.

You're running entire national economies and you still panic over merged cells. The UK lost sixteen thousand COVID cases because someone used your old .xls format and you quietly ran out of rows. No warning. Just vibes.

And VLOOKUP only looks right. Thirty years we spent squinting at #N/A before you finally invented XLOOKUP, like a guy who learns to turn left at fifty.

facts: Invented in 1962 by Sam Panopoulos, a Greek immigrant, at the Satellite Restaurant in Chatham, Ontario, Canada; named after the brand of canned pineapple he used.
Iceland's president Guðni Th. Jóhannesson said in 2017 that he would ban pineapple on pizza if he could, then clarified that a president has no such power.

Hawaii is no longer a major pineapple producer: Del Monte shut its Hawaiian pineapple operations in November 2006, two years ahead of its announced 2008 exit, the state's last cannery closed in 2007, and most canned pineapple now comes from Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines.
Panopoulos, whose restaurant also served Chinese dishes, told the Toronto Sun in 2010 that 'in those days people didn't mix the tastes like sweet and sour, except for Chinese food'.

a.text:
People who order Hawaiian pizza want you to know they're brave. They say "I know, I know" before anyone has said a word, because for them the pineapple isn't a topping, it's a personality. This is a person whose entire rebellious phase fits in a box for $14.99. They've never gotten a tattoo, never quit a job, never sent food back, but once a month they look a teenage cashier dead in the eye and say "pineapple" like they're defusing a bomb.

And they always want to split one with you. Half Hawaiian, half "normal." That's not a compromise. That's a hostage negotiation.

Best part? It isn't even Hawaiian. A Greek guy invented it in Ontario. So congratulations: your one act of rebellion is a Canadian pretending he's on vacation.

b.text:
Hawaiian pizza, you're named after a place you've never been. You were invented in Ontario, by a Greek guy, using canned pineapple. That's not a heritage, that's a witness protection identity.

And the ham? It's Canadian bacon. Even your meat is from Canada. The only Hawaiian thing about you is that people see you and say "aloha," meaning goodbye.

Pineapple has an enzyme that digests protein. You're the only pizza that eats the customer back. Warm fruit juice pooling on mozzarella like a hot tub nobody cleaned.

Italians don't hate you; they pray for you. The president of Iceland said he'd ban you if he could, and Iceland eats fermented shark.

You're not a pizza. You're a fruit cup that fell on a pizza and refused to get up.

facts: Created by linguist Marc Okrand for Star Trek III (1984), building on a few words the actor James Doohan improvised for the 1979 film.
Deliberately alien grammar: object-verb-subject word order and no verb 'to be', so Hamlet's line became 'taH pagh taHbe'', 'continue or not continue'.
The Klingon Language Institute (1992) published Hamlet 'in the original Klingon'; Bing Translator added Klingon in 2013 and Duolingo in 2018.
Okrand's 1985 Klingon Dictionary listed roughly 1,500 words, and fluent speakers number only in the dozens: 20 to 30 in 2009, 30 to 50 by 2018.

a.text: Klingon, you're a language built by one linguist, Marc Okrand, specifically to sound alien and hostile, and somehow you still ended up sounding like a man choking on a Dorito. Your word order is object-verb-subject, so even your sentences walk in backwards to hide their face. You don't even have a word for "hello." Your greeting is "nuqneH," "what do you want?" You're the only language that greets people like a DMV clerk. Your apostrophes are glottal stops, your capital Q is a different letter from lowercase q, and "tlh" isn't a sound, it's a hairball. You translated Hamlet and claimed it was the original. Buddy, the most popular thing ever said in you is "Qapla'," and the people saying it are at a Marriott in Burbank.

b.text: Congratulations on being fluent in Klingon, a language with maybe thirty fluent speakers, and you've met all of them at the same Marriott. You spent four years mastering a tongue where the standard greeting, nuqneH, means "What do you want?" That's also what your family says when you call. You've read Hamlet "restored to the original Klingon," a phrase only a man who has never been hugged could type. One guy raised his son speaking only Klingon; by age five the kid stopped answering him. That's the dream: a language so pure even toddlers refuse it. There's no word for "please," which explains your dating approach. You learned an entire warrior race's language to tell the barista Qapla'. Success. Sure, buddy. Today is a good day to die... a virgin.

facts: A Wi-Fi-connected cold-press juicer launched in 2016 at $699, later cut to $399, that squeezed proprietary bags of chopped produce sold by subscription.
Raised about $120 million from investors including Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins.
In April 2017, Bloomberg reporters squeezed the packs by hand and got 7.5 ounces of juice in 90 seconds, faster than the machine's 8 ounces in about two minutes.
Each pack carried a QR code that the press scanned and checked online before squeezing; it refused expired packs and would not run at all unless connected to Wi-Fi.
Shut down in September 2017 and offered refunds on the machine.

a.text:
Juicero, you were a $400 Wi-Fi-connected juicer that delivered four tons of force, enough, your engineers bragged, to lift two Teslas, and Bloomberg proved the job could be done by a guy with hands. You raised $120 million from Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins to compete with *squeezing*. Every single customer already owned the competing product. It came in pairs.

You sold $8 bags of chopped produce that had to scan a QR code and phone home before you'd juice them. A juicer that needed internet. Imagine the outage: "Sorry, AWS is down, enjoy your sealed pouch of regret." You'd refuse to press an expired pack, like a bouncer for kale.

Doug Evans compared himself to Steve Jobs. Steve Jobs put a thousand songs in your pocket. Doug put a sack of mush in a vise and asked for your Wi-Fi password. Silicon Valley's most expensive way to say, "Just use your hands."

b.text: Four hundred dollars. You paid four hundred dollars so a machine could check with your Wi-Fi before letting you have breakfast. You're the guy who says "disrupt" at Thanksgiving. You didn't want juice; you wanted to be the kind of person a juice startup would pitch to. And it worked! Investors handed that company a hundred and twenty million dollars, and you volunteered to be the exit strategy. Then Bloomberg showed the world you could squeeze the packets with your bare hands, faster, for free. So you paid four hundred dollars to get outperformed by your own grip. Your grandmother squeezed oranges every morning for sixty years. You subscribed to a bag. Somewhere tonight, a router outage stands between a venture capitalist and his kale, and honestly? The router's the smartest thing in that kitchen.

facts: Isolated in 2004 by Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov at Manchester by peeling graphite with Scotch tape; Nobel Prize in Physics, 2010.
The EU's Graphene Flagship, launched in 2013, committed €1 billion over ten years.
A 2018 study in Advanced Materials tested 'graphene' from 60 producers and found none with more than 50% graphene content; most was graphite flakes.
Sold in tennis rackets, running shoes, and headphones as a performance ingredient.
Geim also won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2000 for levitating a frog with magnets.

a.text: Let's hear it for the graphene evangelists, the only people who've been "five years away" since 2004. Two guys in Manchester peel pencil lead with Scotch tape, win a Nobel, and an entire industry decides the tape was the business plan. Every press release is the same Mad Lib: "Wonder material could revolutionize [batteries/condoms/desalination/your feelings]." *Could.* That word has funded more postdocs than the NSF. You promised us space elevators and delivered a tennis racket with a sticker on it. Startup founders slap "graphene-enhanced" on a phone case the way divorced dads put a spoiler on a Honda Civic. And the grant committees keep paying, because admitting the miracle is stuck on the production line means admitting you are too. Twenty years of changing everything, and the only thing you've actually changed is the abstract.

b.text: Graphene, you're one atom thick, and somehow that's still more depth than your business plan. Two hundred times stronger than steel, conducts better than copper, and twenty years later your biggest commercial win is a sticker on a tennis racket. You were discovered with Scotch tape. *Scotch tape!* You're the only Nobel Prize that could've been found in a kindergarten craft drawer. And let's be honest: you're pencil lead that went to grad school. Your cousin graphite has been writing grocery lists for centuries; you've been writing grant proposals. Every year a headline swears you'll revolutionize batteries, chips, water filters. Every year you're still in the lab, like a thirty-year-old in his parents' basement. You can't even be a decent transistor. No bandgap. You literally cannot turn off. Graphene: the material of the future, permanently.

facts: Banned on Singapore's MRT trains and in many Southeast Asian hotels because of the smell.
A 2017 genome study in Nature Genetics traced the odour to a duplicated family of MGL genes that pump out volatile sulfur compounds.

a.text:
People who eat durian in public aren't hungry. They're recruiting. Every bite comes with a sermon: "You just haven't had a *good* one." Sir, I'm on a bus. I didn't ask to join your church.

Singapore fines people for bringing it on the train, and these folks hear that like a dare. They're the only foodies whose restaurant review gets filed as a police report.

And the payoff? Seventy dollars on a Musang King so you can watch strangers silently change seats. You paid premium to become a fire drill. Your date calls it "an acquired taste," which is exactly what you say about someone you're about to break up with.

Then they stroll back to the hotel, walk right past the sign with a red circle through their entire personality, and still act shocked when housekeeping files a complaint.

b.text:
Durian, they call you the King of Fruits, which tracks, because like most monarchies, you stink and nobody's allowed to say it to your face.

You're the only fruit with a criminal record. Banned on the Singapore subway, alongside flammable liquids. Hotels put your picture on signs next to "no smoking." In 2019, a university in Melbourne evacuated five hundred people because they thought there was a gas leak. Nope. Just you, sitting in a cupboard, being yourself.

And the armor! You're covered in spikes like a medieval mace. Nature built you to defend yourself, then gave you a smell that does it better. The spikes are just overkill.

Fans say you taste like custard. Sure. Custard that was left in a gym bag next to some onions. Your flavor isn't an acquired taste. It's a hostage situation.

facts: Oatly started in Sweden in the 1990s, built on Lund University research by Rickard Öste on lactose intolerance.
Oatly's slogan 'It's like milk but made for humans' was banned in Sweden in 2015 after the dairy lobby LRF Mjölk sued; Oatly then published the lawsuit as advertising.
Oatly listed on Nasdaq in May 2021 at a valuation near $10 billion; the shares later lost more than 90% of their value.

Commercial oat milk is made by breaking oat starch into maltose with amylase enzymes, and many brands, Oatly among them, add rapeseed oil; the result has more sugar and a higher glycaemic index than almond or soy milk.

a.text: Let's talk about the oat milk people. You're not lactose intolerant. You've never been tested. You just heard cows are bad and almonds are thirsty, so you picked the one grain that sounds like a farm without the farmer. Congratulations: you pay an extra eighty cents to drink liquid porridge with a splash of rapeseed oil, and you call it "cleaner." You switched from almond the exact week a podcast told you California was in a drought. That's not values, that's a trend with a loyalty card. And the best part? You order it with an air of quiet suffering, like the barista should thank you for saving the planet one Barista Edition carton at a time. Your grandmother ate oats so she could survive winter. You drink them so a stranger in line thinks you've been to therapy.

b.text:
Oat milk, you're porridge that went to finishing school. Somebody looked at horse food and said, "What if it cost seventy cents extra?" Then somebody else said, "Yes, and put it in a carton that talks like a guy who just got back from Copenhagen." Your packaging has more personality than you do. Every box of Oatly reads like a cover letter: "Hi! We're a little weird!" No, you're oats, water, and rapeseed oil. That's not a beverage. That's a salad dressing that gave up.

And the "Barista Edition"? You needed extra oil just to get a job. Enzymes break your starch into maltose, so technically you're a sugar spike in a flannel shirt. Plus you were funded by Blackstone. You're not anti-establishment, oat milk. You're a private equity firm wearing a beanie.

facts: A rice-noodle dish from Liuzhou, Guangxi; the smell comes from pickled bamboo shoots (酸笋), not from the river snails, which only flavour the broth.
The instant version boomed during the 2020 lockdowns; Liuzhou's government reported packaged luosifen sales of over 10 billion yuan that year.
Added to China's national intangible cultural heritage list in 2021.
Liuzhou opened a luosifen industry college in 2020 to train workers for the trade.

Couriers wrap you in four bags like evidence. And you come with seven sachets: chili oil, peanuts, tofu skin, wood ear, the bamboo. It's IKEA furniture that makes the neighbors move out. Liuzhou didn't invent a soup. It invented Stockholm syndrome with chili oil.

They wait until 11 p.m., when the kitchen's empty, like that's a courtesy and not an alibi. They snip open the sour bamboo shoot packet with the focus of a bomb technician, then act shocked when the smoke alarm stays quiet but the flatmates don't. Their entire personality is one sentence, "it tastes way better than it smells," delivered like a TED talk to people holding their breath. facts: The same polymer as Plexiglas and acrylic glass, dissolved in anisole or chlorobenzene and spun into a thin film.

Positive tone: the beam breaks polymer chains and the exposed region dissolves in a MIBK:IPA developer.

Poor dry-etch resistance, so it is used mostly for lift-off rather than as an etch mask.

a.text: PMMA is the same acrylic polymer used in hockey rink glazing, and it has served as a standard electron-beam resist since the 1970s. It can resolve features below 10 nanometers, though this typically requires long exposure times at high dose. Its sensitivity is low, so writing takes substantial beam time. Development usually relies on a mixture of MIBK and IPA, commonly in a one-to-three ratio. PMMA works by chain scission, where exposed regions break into smaller fragments that dissolve in the developer. Excessive dose can cause crosslinking, which reverses its behavior toward negative tone. It has limited resistance to dry etching and degrades in plasma relatively quickly. It performs well in lift-off processes, where its clean removal is a key strength.

b.text: PMMA, you're the same plastic as a hockey rink window, and somehow that's your most dignified job. You've been "high resolution" since the 1970s, which is like bragging about your SAT score at your retirement party. Sure, you'll resolve sub-10-nanometer lines, if someone stands there blasting you with electrons for an eternity. Your sensitivity is so low the beam current has gotten tenure. You don't even develop properly without MIBK and IPA holding your hand in a one-to-three ratio. And your whole personality is chain scission: you literally fall apart when someone pays attention to you. Then hit you with too much dose and you crosslink and flip to negative tone, a full identity crisis. And dry etch? You melt in plasma faster than an ice sculpture at a barbecue. Honestly, the only thing you're consistently good at is lift-off: leaving.

Every year you rewrite your whole app in a new framework, then bolt on TypeScript so you can pretend you chose a real language.

facts: Launched by Ty Inc. in 1993 and sold only through small gift shops, with designs 'retired' to manufacture scarcity.

At the height of the craze Beanie Babies accounted for about 10% of eBay's sales, and eBay's 1998 IPO filing said the site at times had over 30,000 Beanie Baby auctions running simultaneously in the quarter ending June 1998.
In 1999 a divorcing couple divided their Beanie Baby collection one by one on a courtroom floor, in a photograph that ran worldwide.
In 1999 Ty announced that Beanie Babies would be retired at the end of the year, then reversed itself after asking the public to vote and seeing an overwhelming vote to keep them.
Most 'rare' Beanies that price guides valued in the thousands now sell for a few dollars.

a.text: Let's hear it for the Beanie Baby investors, the only people who bought a retirement plan at a Hallmark store. You put tag protectors on a heart-shaped piece of cardboard and called it diversification. You drove to four McDonald's for Teenie Beanies, threw away the Happy Meals, and told your kids it was for their college fund. Now that kid is thirty, still paying off loans, and his inheritance is a Rubbermaid tub of Princess the Bears. Every few months you see an eBay listing asking $500,000 for one with a tag typo and think, "Vindicated." Babe, that's not a market. That's another guy in another garage, also lying to his wife. Ty Warner told you which ones were "retired," and you believed him. Ty Warner later pleaded guilty to hiding money offshore. He hoarded too. He just hoarded the right thing.

b.text:
Beanie Babies, look at you. Half bear, half beanbag, all retirement plan that never paid out. An entire generation of parents bought you instead of index funds. Somewhere a man is still storing Princess, the purple Diana bear, in a climate-controlled unit, waiting for the market to "recover." Buddy, the market recovered. It just didn't take you with it.

Your most valuable feature was a heart-shaped paper tag. People bought plastic tag protectors. For the tag. That's like buying a phone case for your receipt.

And every tag had a little poem rhyming "bear" with "care." Hallmark called that lazy.

A Las Vegas couple had to divide you on a courtroom floor during their divorce, one at a time. That's the most anyone has wanted you since 1999: only to make sure their ex didn't get you.

Ty Warner got a billion dollars. You got plastic pellets.

facts: Oatly started in Sweden in the 1990s, built on Lund University research by Rickard Öste on lactose intolerance.
Oatly's slogan 'It's like milk but made for humans' was banned in Sweden in 2015 after the dairy lobby LRF Mjölk sued; Oatly then published the lawsuit as advertising.
Oatly listed on Nasdaq in May 2021 at a valuation near $10 billion; the shares later lost more than 90% of their value.

Commercial oat milk is made by breaking oat starch into maltose with amylase enzymes, and many brands, Oatly among them, add rapeseed oil; the result has more sugar and a higher glycaemic index than almond or soy milk.

a.text:
Oat milk, you're porridge that went to finishing school. Somebody looked at horse food and said, "What if it cost seventy cents extra?" Then somebody else said, "Yes, and put it in a carton that talks like a guy who just got back from Copenhagen." Your packaging has more personality than you do. Every box of Oatly reads like a cover letter: "Hi! We're a little weird!" No, you're oats, water, and rapeseed oil. That's not a beverage. That's a salad dressing that gave up.

And the "Barista Edition"? You needed extra oil just to get a job. Enzymes break your starch into maltose, so technically you're a sugar spike in a flannel shirt. Plus you were funded by Blackstone. You're not anti-establishment, oat milk. You're a private equity firm wearing a beanie.

b.text:
Oat milk people, let's be honest: you're not lactose intolerant. I've watched you eat a whole burrata at brunch. You switched because almond milk got canceled for drinking California dry, and you needed a new personality before anyone noticed you'd had the old one for six years.

You pay eighty cents extra to drink breakfast. Your grandma ate oats so she could afford milk. You're paying more for oats so you can say "I just find it creamier."

And you tell the barista "barista edition, if you have it," like you're ordering a vintage. Same person who reads every label hunting for seed oils. Guess what's in your porridge latte, Kayleigh? Rapeseed oil.

You didn't save the planet. You flew to Lisbon twice this year. You just found a way to sigh at a cow.

You wear them barefoot, so by February they smell like a wet lamb's final wish. They're as waterproof as a muffin. Oprah put them on her Favorite Things list. She's since moved on. And the walk: your ankles gave up years ago and went horizontal. You're not walking anymore, you're leaning toward your destination. Australian surfers wore these to warm up after the freezing ocean. facts: Created at Pizzeria Uno in Chicago in 1943; credit is disputed among founder Ike Sewell, his partner Ric Riccardo, and cook Rudy Malnati.
Assembled upside down: sliced mozzarella on the dough, then toppings, then crushed tomatoes on top, so the cheese does not scorch during the long bake.
Jon Stewart called it 'tomato soup in a bread bowl' and 'a casserole' on The Daily Show in 2013.

Chicagoans' everyday pizza is thin 'tavern-style' cut into squares; GrubHub order data reported by WBEZ in 2013 showed city residents ordering non-deep-dish pizza about 10 to 1 over deep dish, with deep dish and stuffed making up under 9% of orders.

a.text: Chicago deep-dish isn't a pizza. It's a casserole that got a fake ID. You order it, and the waiter says, "That'll be forty-five minutes." Forty-five minutes! I've had relationships bake faster. They put the sauce on top because if you saw what was underneath first, you'd leave. A solid sheet of sausage, like somebody paved a driveway with a patty. Two pounds of mozzarella hiding under a tomato quilt. It's not a slice, it's a core sample. You need a knife, a fork, and a structural engineer. The crust is buttery cornmeal, so it's a pie crust, so congratulations, you're eating dessert with ambitions. And here's the best part: actual Chicagoans don't even eat it. They eat tavern-style thin crust cut in squares. Deep-dish is just the city's way of keeping tourists too full to walk to Wrigley.

b.text: Let's talk about the people who insist deep-dish is pizza. Mostly Chicagoans with a Second City complex so severe they'll defend anything New York makes fun of. Jon Stewart called it a casserole in 2013, and half of Lincoln Park still hasn't emotionally recovered. These are folks who order, then wait forty-five minutes at Lou Malnati's, and call that patience instead of what it is: a hostage negotiation with a buzzer. They eat it with a knife and fork and still claim it's the same food you fold on a subway platform. And what does it get them? A Giordano's line full of tourists from Ohio, a nap at 2 p.m., and the right to lecture you about tavern-style, which, notice, is what they actually eat at home. Defending deep-dish isn't civic pride. It's Stockholm syndrome with a parking ticket.

facts: Hydrogen silsesquioxane, sold by Dow Corning as FOx ('flowable oxide') and designed as a spin-on dielectric for chip interconnects; lithographers adopted it as a negative-tone resist.
Exposure converts its cage structure into a cross-linked, silica-like network, so the developed pattern is essentially SiO2.
Holds the resolution records for electron-beam lithography: isolated features around 5 nm, dense lines below 10 nm half-pitch, with high-contrast 'salty' NaOH/NaCl development.

Must be kept refrigerated (Dow Corning's datasheet gives a six-month shelf life at 5 °C); the solution ages into a jelly, and its effective sensitivity shifts with processing delays because cross-linking continues after exposure.

DuPont, which inherited Dow Corning's FOx/XR-1541 HSQ line, discontinued it and ended production at the end of 2025; labs such as EPFL's CMi switched to third-party HSQ from EM Resist or DisChem, both formulated from AQM powder.

a.text: So you switched to HSQ for the resolution. Bold move for someone whose devices still die at wire bonding. You saw one SEM of 6-nanometer lines at a conference and decided PMMA was beneath you. Now you're writing at a dose so high your name sits on the e-beam calendar like a hostage note. Your resist lives in the fridge next to somebody's yogurt, and you check its age more often than your own. You develop in salt water now, the closest you've come to a beach in three years. And congratulations on those gorgeous lines. They're basically glass, so the only way to fix a mistake is HF, a fume hood, and a long call to your mother. All this for one inset figure the reviewer will ask you to make bigger.

b.text:
HSQ, ladies and gentlemen: the only resist with sub-10-nanometer resolution and the personality of a sourdough starter. You buy it, you refrigerate it, and it *still* starts gelling in the bottle like it's got somewhere better to be. Shelf life measured in "eh, few months, maybe."

And slow? HSQ needs a dose so high the e-beam tool files for overtime. Your PMMA friends finished their write and went home; you're still exposing alignment marks.

Then you develop it in TMAH, or, if you want contrast, *salty* developer. Yes, this resist literally needs you to add salt. Even Gordon Ramsay thinks that's a lot.

But the real red flag? Once it's exposed, it turns into glass. Permanently. You want it gone? Hydrofluoric acid. That's not a resist, that's a relationship you can only leave with a hazmat suit.

Still, gorgeous lines. Shame they collapse when they dry.

b.text:
Chicago deep-dish pizza, everybody! facts: Began in 1976 as a set of macros for the TECO editor at MIT's AI Lab, written by Richard Stallman and others; GNU Emacs followed in 1985.
Extensible in its own Lisp dialect, Emacs Lisp; the standing joke is that it is a fine operating system lacking only a good editor.
Ships with a psychotherapist (M-x doctor), Tetris, a mail client, a calendar, and a web browser (eww).
An old backronym is 'Eight Megabytes And Constantly Swapping', from when 8 MB was a lot of memory.
'Emacs pinky' is the name for the hand strain blamed on its Control-key chords.

a.text:
Emacs is the only text editor that ships with a psychotherapist, and you'll need it. M-x doctor exists because the developers knew exactly what they were doing to people.

It's a great operating system. It has a mail client, a web browser, Tetris, and a Lisp interpreter. What it lacks is a decent text editor. Its most beloved package is Evil mode, which is just Vim wearing an Emacs costume. That's like buying a Ferrari and installing a horse.

Want to save? C-x C-s. Want to quit? C-x C-c. Want to feel your left pinky again? Too late. Emacs stands for "Escape Meta Alt Control Shift," and the RSI stands for "you chose this."

Every user has a 4,000-line init.el they don't understand, copied from strangers on Stack Overflow in 2009.

b.text: You people don't use Emacs, you move into it, like a guy who rents a storage unit and starts getting mail there. You read email in mu4e, browse in eww, run a shell in eshell, and when you finally crack, you M-x doctor and tell a Lisp therapist your feelings. Your init.el is four thousand lines, half commented out, and you've declared Emacs bankruptcy twice: the only bankruptcy that ever made someone feel superior. You spent a weekend cutting startup from 1.8 seconds to 0.9, on a program you never close. Your left pinky is shot from holding Control, a war wound from never touching a mouse. Your whole life is in Org-mode, including a habit tracker whose only entry is "configure habit tracker." And that novel you built the perfect writing environment for? It's in there too. Under TODO.

facts: Hand-drawn by Chris Costello in 1982 over about six months, when he was 23; he sold the rights to Letraset for $750.
Bundled with macOS and with Microsoft Office, which is why it appears on so many menus and signs.
James Cameron's Avatar (2009) used it for the film's logo and subtitles.
A 2017 Saturday Night Live sketch starring Ryan Gosling is about a man unable to get over that choice.

a.text: Papyrus, you were designed in 1982 by a 23-year-old with calligraphy pens and a dream of ancient Egypt, and somehow you still look like you were drawn by someone shivering. Your edges are so rough you need exfoliating. You promised the wisdom of the Nile and delivered the vibe of a chiropractor's tri-fold brochure. Every day spa, hookah lounge, and "Inner Journey" yoga retreat found you in the dropdown menu and whispered, "This feels ancient." James Cameron spent $237 million on *Avatar* and then used you for the logo, which is like building the Taj Mahal and signing it in crayon. Ryan Gosling lost sleep over you on national television. You're not a typeface; you're a cry for help with ragged little serifs. Even Comic Sans looks at you and says, "At least I know I'm a joke."

b.text: You opened a day spa. You wanted serenity, wisdom, a whisper of the Nile. So you scrolled the font menu, sailed past Comic Sans feeling very sophisticated, and stopped on the one James Cameron used to title a billion-dollar movie. Congratulations: your sign now says "ancient healing" exactly as loudly as your aunt's church potluck flyer. Every hummus joint, every reiki studio, every tea shop run by a man named River made this same choice, alone, convinced they'd discovered it. The guy who designed it was twenty-three and has spent forty years apologizing. You paid a contractor to carve his apology into cedar. You wanted customers to feel transported. They do: straight back to 2003, a Word document, and a fourth grader typing "Spring Bake Sale." Cucumber water not included.

facts: The largest fruit that grows on a tree; single fruits can weigh over 40 kg.
The national fruit of Bangladesh and the state fruit of Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
Unripe flesh is sold as a vegan 'pulled pork' substitute, although it has only 1-2 g of protein per 100 g.
Cutting one releases a sticky white latex, so cooks oil their knives and hands first.
A member of the mulberry family (Moraceae), a relative of breadfruit and figs.

a.text:
Let's talk about the geniuses selling jackfruit as "pulled pork." These are people who looked at a fruit that half of Kerala has been feeding to cousins for free since forever, slapped it in a brine pouch, and charged eleven dollars for the privilege of being disappointed in a Whole Foods.

Their whole business model is barbecue sauce. That's it. They're a sauce company with a fruit alibi. And when you mention it has about two grams of protein, they get *defensive*. Buddy, you sold me a pork sandwich with the nutritional profile of a pear.

But I get the appeal. You don't need a lab, a patent, or a scientist named Klaus. You just need a food truck, a beard, and the confidence to say "same texture!" to people who haven't eaten pork since 2011 and genuinely can't remember.

b.text:
Jackfruit, look at you. The largest fruit that grows on a tree, and you couldn't even make it to the branches. You just hang off the trunk like a drunk uncle clinging to a lamppost.

You weigh eighty pounds. That's not a fruit, that's a fourth grader in a bumpy green costume. People cut you open and need cooking oil on their hands and knives, because your insides are basically rubber cement. You're the only produce that requires a solvent.

And vegans love you because when you're young, you taste like absolutely nothing. Your big career move is pretending to be pulled pork. Your whole identity is "not bad if you drown me in barbecue sauce."

Then you ripen and smell like Juicy Fruit gum fermenting in a gym bag.

You're the national fruit of Bangladesh, and you still find time to fall on people's heads.

facts: Tofu soaked for hours to a day or two in a brine that has itself fermented for months from vegetables such as bamboo shoots and mustard greens, often with dried shrimp or meat; the smell is the brine's, not the bean's.

Changsha's version is black, deep-fried and doused in chili; Taiwan's night-market version is golden and served with pickled cabbage; Shaoxing's, brined with amaranth stalks, is fried pale yellow or steamed with other 'stinky' pickles.
Legend credits Wang Zhihe, a Qing-era exam candidate who left his unsold tofu too long in 1669; a Beijing fermented-bean-curd brand still carries his name.
Street vendors are its main outlet, and the smell carries for a block.

a.text:
Let's talk about the stinky tofu people. You smelled it from three blocks away, a smell like a sewer filed a noise complaint, and your brain said: *that's where we're eating.* Your entire personality is "it tastes better than it smells." That's not a review. That's a hostage statement.

You stand on a Taipei night market curb with a paper boat, chopsticks in one hand, phone in the other, filming your own bravery for followers who can't smell it, which is the only reason they're still following you. Tourists do it once for the story. Locals do it every Tuesday, then board the MRT, where forty strangers silently agree to hate them.

And the pickled cabbage on top? That's you pretending you came for vegetables. You didn't. You came to be the deadliest passenger on the scooter.

b.text: Stinky tofu, you're the only food that announces itself before the menu does. People find you at the night market the way sharks find blood: follow the stench three stalls past the bubble tea. Your brine is fermented vegetables, shrimp, amaranth stems, and apparently a gym sock that lost a bet. Months in that bucket, and you came out smelling like a festival porta-potty in August. Your own name is a confession. Not "aged tofu," not "artisanal bean curd." Your family took one whiff and went, "Yeah, call him Stinky." And the Changsha version? Dyed jet black, like it's in mourning for everyone's sense of smell. The only reason anyone finishes you is the pickled cabbage and chili sauce piled on top to keep you quiet. "Smells bad, tastes good" isn't a slogan, buddy. It's a hostage negotiation.

facts: Created at Pizzeria Uno in Chicago in 1943; credit is disputed among founder Ike Sewell, his partner Ric Riccardo, and cook Rudy Malnati.
Assembled upside down: sliced mozzarella on the dough, then toppings, then crushed tomatoes on top, so the cheese does not scorch during the long bake.
Jon Stewart called it 'tomato soup in a bread bowl' and 'a casserole' on The Daily Show in 2013.

Chicagoans' everyday pizza is thin 'tavern-style' cut into squares; GrubHub order data reported by WBEZ in 2013 showed city residents ordering non-deep-dish pizza about 10 to 1 over deep dish, with deep dish and stuffed making up under 9% of orders.

a.text: Chicago deep-dish isn't a pizza. It's a casserole with a publicist. You order one and the waiter says "forty-five minutes," which is how long it takes to bake and also how long it takes to finish one slice. They put the sauce on top and the cheese underneath, like they're hiding evidence. That's not a recipe, that's a cover-up. The crust is a buttery retaining wall holding back a lake of chunky tomato, because apparently Lake Michigan wasn't enough water for one city to manage. You need a knife, a fork, a nap, and a cardiologist on retainer. Then there's the sausage, laid down as one solid patty like the base layer of a parking garage. Chicagoans defend it like family. Sure: the relative who shows up late, takes up three chairs, and leaves everyone unable to move.

b.text: Let's talk about the people who insist deep-dish is pizza. You're from the city that named its own comedy theater Second City and still acts shocked when nobody ranks you first. You're not defending food. You're nursing a grudge against New York you've carried since losing the World's Fair argument and the skyline argument. You'll wait forty-five minutes at Lou Malnati's, order before you're seated like it's the DMV, then ask for a knife and fork and call it "the real thing." Jon Stewart roasted you on national TV and you took it personally, because deep down you knew he was right. You ship it on dry ice to your cousin in Phoenix like an organ donation. And what does the label get you? Navy Pier tourists nodding politely, a two-hour nap, and the Midwest's loudest participation trophy.

facts: John Sylvan invented the K-Cup in the early 1990s and sold his stake for about $50,000 in 1997; in 2015 he told The Atlantic, 'I feel bad sometimes that I ever did it.'
Keurig 2.0 (2014) read an ink mark on the lid and rejected unlicensed pods; sales fell and workarounds spread online.
By 2014 enough K-Cups were sold each year to circle the Earth more than ten times; the pods were mostly unrecyclable #7 plastic until a switch to polypropylene by 2020.
Keurig Green Mountain merged with Dr Pepper Snapple in 2018 to form Keurig Dr Pepper.

a.text:
Keurig, you took the simplest drink in human history (hot water, beans) and added a subscription model. Your own inventor said he regrets making you. Imagine your dad publicly apologizing for you and you're still in every dentist's waiting room.

You tried DRM on coffee. Keurig 2.0 literally scanned pods and refused to brew anything off-brand. You're the only appliance that's ever asked me for a license.

Every K-Cup costs more per pound than a decent steak, and you've buried enough of them to circle the Earth a dozen times. Archaeologists will dig them up and assume we worshipped tiny plastic thimbles.

And the Keurig Kold? A $370 soda machine that died faster than the flat Coke it made.

Your descale light blinks like a cry for help. Honestly, same.

b.text: Keurig people want coffee the way they want feelings: one serving, sealed, no cleanup. You're not a coffee drinker, you're a pod collector. You bought the variety pack, and now you're thirty-eight, rationing the last Donut Shop because all that's left is hazelnut and a hot cocoa you're saving for a breakdown. You press "Strong" like it's a personality trait. You swore you'd use the reusable filter, and you bought one. It's in a drawer next to your gym key fob. You saved four whole minutes, and you spend them staring at a blinking descale light you've decided is decorative. The guy who invented the pod publicly regrets it. You built your mornings around a man's biggest apology. Enjoy your landfill latte, champ. Ready in sixty seconds, just like your effort.

facts: Reported by Sumio Iijima in Nature in 1991.
Promised as the cable for a space elevator; a 2006 analysis showed that ordinary defects cut the strength of a macroscopic cable far below the ideal value.
Long, rigid multi-walled nanotubes behaved like asbestos fibres in a 2008 mouse study in Nature Nanotechnology.
Sorting metallic from semiconducting tubes has blocked nanotube electronics for three decades; MIT's 16-bit RV16X-NANO processor (2019) is still a lab demonstration.
Today they are sold mainly as a conductive additive in lithium-ion battery electrodes.

a.text:
Carbon nanotubes, everybody! The only material that's been "five years away" since 1991. You're a hundred times stronger than steel, and you've used that strength to hold together... a tennis racket. They promised us a space elevator; you can't get past a few centimeters without a defect. That's not a cable, that's a toothpick with a press agent.

You're basically graphene that rolled itself up out of insecurity, and graphene still got the Nobel. Your cousin the buckyball got one too. You got a shoutout in a bike-frame brochure.

You can't even decide if you're a metal or a semiconductor; it depends on the angle you got rolled at. You clump together like nerds at a mixer, and the second you escape, you lodge in lungs like asbestos. Strongest thing on Earth, and your best trick is ending up in a safety data sheet.

b.text: Let's hear it for the carbon nanotube founders, the only people who've been "five years from commercialization" since 1991. You can spot them at any pitch day: a postdoc in a blazer that still smells like the clean room, opening with a space elevator and closing with a seed round. Bold move, promising a cable to orbit when your entire production run fits in a vial labeled "DO NOT INHALE." They swear they'll replace silicon. Silicon has heard this every year since Clinton and keeps shipping. They say "a hundred times stronger than steel" the way your uncle says he could've gone pro. And what does it get them? A Nature cover, a term sheet, and a quiet pivot to "conductive additive for batteries." The dream: a ladder to space. The exit: slightly better tennis rackets.

facts: Beeple's 'Everydays: The First 5000 Days' sold at Christie's for $69.3 million in March 2021.
OpenSea, the largest NFT marketplace, processed a record $2.7 billion in trades on 1 May 2022 and just $9.34 million on 28 August 2022, a 99% drop, according to DappRadar data.
A 2023 dappGambl study found that 95% of the NFT collections it examined had a market value of zero.
The token usually records only a URL; the image itself sits on an ordinary server or IPFS, not on the blockchain.
Collins Dictionary named 'NFT' its word of the year for 2021.

a.text: Let's hear it for the 2021 NFT buyer. You paid four hundred dollars in gas fees to become the legal owner of something your coworker right-click saved during the meeting where you explained it. You didn't want art. You've never wanted art. You wanted a hexagon around your Twitter picture so strangers would know you had a Discord password. You typed "WAGMI" to eleven thousand anonymous cartoon monkeys and believed it. We are not all gonna make it, Kyle. The roadmap promised a metaverse yacht party; it delivered a founder named "0xDegenSensei" who deleted his account and moved to Portugal. But hey, you got what you paid for: a floor price you check like a heart monitor, and a profile picture you still can't bring yourself to change, because then it would be over.

b.text:
NFTs, you're the only investment where the product is a receipt, and the receipt is a link to a JPEG hosted on some guy's server. When he stops paying the bill, congratulations: you own a 404.

You convinced grown adults to pay $300,000 for a cartoon monkey in a sailor hat, then charge them $80 in gas fees to watch it lose 98% of its value. Jimmy Fallon showed off his ape on national television like a kid holding up a cool rock.

People right-clicked and hit "save as," and you called it theft. Theft of *what*? It's still there! I'm looking at it!

Every project had a roadmap: metaverse, merch, a members-only yacht party. Instead the roadmap was a Discord mod named Kevin typing "we're still early" at 3 a.m.

WAGMI, you said. We did not all make it.

facts: The same polymer as Plexiglas and acrylic glass, dissolved in anisole or chlorobenzene and spun into a thin film.
The oldest electron-beam resist still in everyday use; IBM researchers reported it as one in the late 1960s.
Positive tone: the beam breaks polymer chains and the exposed region dissolves in a MIBK:IPA developer.
Resolves below 10 nm but has poor sensitivity, so doses of hundreds to over a thousand µC/cm² (depending on voltage) make writing slow.
Poor dry-etch resistance, so it is used mostly for lift-off rather than as an etch mask.

a.text: You people still spinning PMMA aren't doing lithography. You're doing historical reenactment. Your advisor's advisor scribbled the recipe on a napkin in 1975, and you treat it like scripture: 950K over 495K, MIBK to IPA one-to-three, develop sixty seconds while whispering to the beaker. You tell everyone it's about "resolution." It's about nobody wanting to file the purchase order for ZEP. So you crank the dose until writing one chip takes longer than your stipend lasts, then discover your pattern won't survive ten seconds in the etcher. So you do liftoff, because of course you do. Your entire thesis is gold rectangles. You're not a nanofabrication researcher. You're the guy who knows which bottle in the cleanroom is "the good IPA" and guards it like a dragon.

b.text:
PMMA, you're literally Plexiglas. Somewhere your cousin is a sneeze guard at Chipotle, and honestly? Your cousin has better etch resistance. One whiff of plasma and you vanish faster than a grad student's weekend.

You've been the "gold standard" since the 1970s, which is a polite way of saying nobody's been able to fire you. You need hundreds of microcoulombs just to *notice* the beam. A 40-hour write for one wafer. Glacial, but sure, sub-10-nanometer lines, we get it.

Positive resist? Overdose you and you cross-link into a *negative* one. That's not versatility, that's an identity crisis.

You get developed in MIBK, which smells like regret, and you come in 495K and 950K because one of you alone can't even do liftoff. And acetone dissolves you instantly. Even your solvents think you're temporary.

facts: Descends from Lizzie Magie's The Landlord's Game, patented in 1904 to teach the evils of land monopoly in the spirit of Henry George.
Charles Darrow sold his version to Parker Brothers in 1935 and was credited as the inventor; Parker bought Magie's patent for $500.
The official rules require any unbought property to be auctioned, and 'Free Parking' pays nothing; the house rules that skip the auction and pile cash on Free Parking are why games drag.
During the Second World War, British intelligence had maps, compasses, and real currency hidden in sets sent to prisoner-of-war camps.

a.text: Let's talk about families who still play Monopoly on holidays. You know who you are: you swore it'd be "fun," then spent four hours watching your brother-in-law build hotels on Boardwalk like he's finally getting the respect his career never gave him. Dad's the banker, which means a man with zero accountability and a lap full of orange five-hundreds. Mom invented a Free Parking jackpot rule in 1994 and will defend it harder than her marriage. Your little cousin traded you Park Place for Baltic and "a favor later," and somehow that's the most binding contract in your family. Nobody's ever finished a game. It ends the same way every year: someone flips the board, someone cries in jail, and Grandma pockets the Get Out of Jail Free card like she's been planning it since Nixon.

b.text:
Monopoly, you were invented by Lizzie Magie to teach people that landlords ruin lives, and somehow the lesson everyone learned was "buy Park Place." Then Parker Brothers bought you from a guy who basically stole you, which is the most on-brand origin story in history.

You're the only game where "second prize in a beauty contest" counts as income and jail is solved with a coupon. Your mascot looks like he foreclosed on the Pringles guy, and half of America swears he wears a monocle. He doesn't. We just assumed a man that rich would be hiding something.

Nobody has ever finished you. Games don't end; your cousin just flips the board over Marvin Gardens, which you misspelled, by the way. It's Marven. Even your real estate is a scam.

a.text: PMMA, you're the same plastic as a hockey rink window, and somehow that's your most dignified job. You've been "high resolution" since the 1970s, which is like bragging about your SAT score at your retirement party. Sure, you'll resolve sub-10-nanometer lines, if someone stands there blasting you with electrons for an eternity. Your sensitivity is so low the beam current has gotten tenure. You don't even develop properly without MIBK and IPA holding your hand in a one-to-three ratio. And your whole personality is chain scission: you literally fall apart when someone pays attention to you. Then hit you with too much dose and you crosslink and flip to negative tone, a full identity crisis. And dry etch? You melt in plasma faster than an ice sculpture at a barbecue. Honestly, the only thing you're consistently good at is lift-off: leaving.

b.text:
PMMA, you're the same plastic as a hockey rink window, and somehow that's your most dignified job. You've been "high resolution" since the 1970s, which is like bragging about your SAT score at your retirement party. Sure, you'll resolve sub-10-nanometer lines, if someone stands there blasting you with electrons for an eternity. Your sensitivity is so low the beam current has gotten tenure. You don't even develop properly without MIBK and IPA holding your hand in a one-to-three ratio. And your whole personality is chain scission: you literally fall apart when someone pays attention to you. Then hit you with too much dose and you crosslink and flip to negative tone, a full identity crisis. And dry etch? You melt in plasma faster than an ice sculpture at a barbecue. Honestly, the only thing you're consistently good at is lift-off: leaving.

The joke relies on a double meaning of "leaving": in lift-off, a common nanofabrication process, metal is deposited over patterned PMMA, and dissolving the resist beneath it removes the unwanted metal along with the resist, so the PMMA literally leaves the scene. Because PMMA's departure is the intended outcome of that step, the punchline turns its one reliable skill into a backhanded compliment.

facts: Released in October 2012; removed the Start button and booted into a full-screen grid of tiles designed for touch screens most PCs did not have.
The 8.1 update in 2013 put a Start button back, Windows 10 (2015) restored the Start menu, and Microsoft skipped the name Windows 9 altogether.

Microsoft dropped the 'Metro' name in August 2012 after reports that German retailer Metro AG had objected on trademark grounds; Microsoft called 'Metro' a code name and denied any litigation, and the style was afterwards known informally as 'Modern UI'.
The 'Charms bar' hid Search, Share, and Settings behind an invisible swipe from the right edge.
Windows RT, the ARM edition launched alongside it, could not run ordinary Windows programs; Microsoft wrote down $900 million of unsold Surface RT tablets in 2013.

a.text: Windows 8, Microsoft looked at the Start button, the one thing every human on Earth knew how to use, and said, "What if we hid it?" You turned every desktop into a giant tablet nobody could touch. People were swiping at their monitors like they were wiping off a stain. Shutting you down required a treasure map: hover in a corner, summon the Charms bar, Settings, Power. Charms! Like the operating system was a bracelet from Claire's. You shipped with two Internet Explorers, which is two more than anyone wanted. Even your design name, Metro, got taken away by lawyers. And when 8.1 finally brought the Start button back, it just took you to the same tile screen. That's not an apology, that's a hostage note. You were so bad Microsoft skipped Windows 9 entirely, just to put more distance between us and you.

b.text: Windows 8, Microsoft looked at the Start button, the one thing every human on Earth knew how to use, and said, "What if we hid it?" You turned every desktop into a giant tablet nobody could touch. People were swiping at their monitors like they were wiping off a stain. Shutting you down required a treasure map: hover in a corner, summon the Charms bar, Settings, Power. Charms! Like the operating system was a bracelet from Claire's. You shipped with two Internet Explorers, which is two more than anyone wanted. Even your design name, Metro, got taken away by lawyers. And when 8.1 finally brought the Start button back, it just took you to the same tile screen. That's not an apology, that's a hostage note. You were so bad Microsoft skipped Windows 9 entirely, just to put more distance between us and you. Microsoft's next major release after Windows 8 was named Windows 10, so the number 9 never appeared. The joke exaggerates that naming choice by presenting it as a deliberate escape from the Windows 8 name.

facts: Unveiled at Google I/O 2012 with skydivers livestreaming their jump through it onto the Moscone Center roof.
The Explorer Edition sold to invited users in 2013 for $1,500.
Wearers were nicknamed 'Glassholes'; bars, cinemas, and casinos banned the device over its camera.
The consumer programme ended in January 2015; an Enterprise Edition continued until Google stopped selling it in 2023.
Its display was a 640-by-360 prism in the corner of one eye.

a.text: Google Glass, you cost fifteen hundred dollars and made everyone wearing you look like a Bluetooth headset that got promoted. Sergey Brin launched you by skydiving onto a building, and that's the last time you were ever cool. You put a tiny prism over one eye so people could check email while pretending to make eye contact. You didn't invent a computer, you invented a reason to get punched. You're the only gadget that gave us a new slur: "Glasshole." Bars banned you. Movie theaters banned you. Robert Scoble wore you in the shower, and that photo did more damage than any privacy lawsuit. You took pictures when people winked, turning every awkward conversation into a potential felony. Your battery died before your reputation did, and that's impressive. Rest in peace: demoted to warehouse work, then quietly killed in 2023. The most Google ending possible.

b.text: Look at this guy. Paid fifteen hundred dollars to join the Explorer Program, and the only thing he's explored is the sidewalk outside every bar in San Francisco. He walks up and says "OK Glass" out loud, like a man ordering from a butler who isn't there. You came here to meet women, and you're the one person every woman in the room has already assumed is filming her. Buddy, when you wink at someone, she doesn't think you're flirting. She thinks you just took her picture. Because you did. You tap your temple like you're having a thought, and we all know you've never had one. Google gave up on you. Google, the company that kept Google+ alive for eight years, looked at you and said "no." There's a word for you. It's Glasshole, and you earned it.

facts: Released in February 2024 at $3,499, with an external battery pack on a cable rated for about two hours.
'EyeSight' shows a rendering of the wearer's eyes on an outward-facing screen.
Apple calls it 'spatial computing' and its App Store rules tell developers not to describe apps as AR, VR, XR, or MR.
Reports during 2024 said Apple had cut production; analysts' first-year sales estimates were well under a million units.
Weighs 600-650 g, before the battery.

a.text: Apple Vision Pro, everybody! Thirty-five hundred dollars to look like a scuba diver lost in a Best Buy. Apple insists it's not VR, it's "spatial computing," which is like calling a fanny pack "hip luggage." It's so heavy they had to throw in a second strap, and the battery's a separate brick on a cord, so you're basically a lamp that walks. Two hours of charge! That's not a computer, that's a matinee. Then there's EyeSight, the screen that shows your eyes on the front, so your family can watch a dim, blurry you stare at nothing. Most honest feature Apple's ever made. Netflix wouldn't even make an app. Netflix! They're on smart fridges! And your Persona looks like a hostage video filmed inside the uncanny valley.

b.text: You paid thirty-five hundred dollars to ride the 6 train inside Joshua Tree. Everyone else has to smell the actual 6 train; you just hear it echoing through a desert like a ghost with a MetroCard. You want us to know you're an early adopter. We know. Your little cartoon eyes are blinking at us like a hostage video. That cable running to your pocket says "the future" and also "IV drip." You pinch the air at Union Square and a stranger thinks you're ordering him to move. You've got a hundred-foot Mac screen floating over a man eating soup out of a Pringles can. And the battery dies in two hours, so you'll still get to experience the subway in full, unimmersive 3D. Your commute outlasts your device. Welcome back to reality. It's delayed.

facts: Isolated in 2004 by Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov at Manchester by peeling graphite with Scotch tape; Nobel Prize in Physics, 2010.
The EU's Graphene Flagship, launched in 2013, committed €1 billion over ten years.
A 2018 study in Advanced Materials tested 'graphene' from 60 producers and found none with more than 50% graphene content; most was graphite flakes.
Sold in tennis rackets, running shoes, and headphones as a performance ingredient.
Geim also won an Ig Nobel Prize in 2000 for levitating a frog with magnets.

a.text:
Graphene, you're the only Nobel Prize winner ever discovered with Scotch tape. Two physicists peeled a pencil and found you, which means your origin story is literally "kid procrastinating on homework."

Since 2004 you've been "about to revolutionize" batteries, computers, water filters, and space elevators. Twenty years later your biggest commercial win is a tennis racket. You're not a wonder material, you're a press release with a hexagon fetish.

Everyone loves to say you're two hundred times stronger than steel. Great. You're also one atom thick. Nobody's impressed that a sheet of paper beats a battleship per ounce.

And for the supposed savior of electronics, you have zero bandgap. You can't even turn off. You're a transistor with no off switch, the guy at the party who never stops talking.

You're graphite with a LinkedIn profile.

b.text: Let's hear it for the graphene evangelists, the only people who've been "five years away" since 2004. Two guys in Manchester peel pencil lead with Scotch tape, win a Nobel, and an entire industry decides the tape was the business plan. Every press release is the same Mad Lib: "Wonder material could revolutionize [batteries/condoms/desalination/your feelings]." *Could.* That word has funded more postdocs than the NSF. You promised us space elevators and delivered a tennis racket with a sticker on it. Startup founders slap "graphene-enhanced" on a phone case the way divorced dads put a spoiler on a Honda Civic. And the grant committees keep paying, because admitting the miracle is stuck on the production line means admitting you are too. Twenty years of changing everything, and the only thing you've actually changed is the abstract.

facts: Released by Bram Moolenaar in November 1991 as 'Vi IMitation', a vi clone he had begun writing for the Amiga in 1988 on top of Stevie; the expansion became 'Vi IMproved' with version 2.0 in December 1993.
Licensed as charityware: the licence asks users to donate to ICCF Holland, a charity Moolenaar ran for children in Uganda.
Stack Overflow's question 'How to exit the Vim editor?' passed one million visits in May 2017, which Stack Overflow marked with a blog post.
Modal editing: in normal mode, typing letters runs commands rather than inserting text; :wq saves and quits, :q! quits and discards changes.

a.text: You know a Vim user is in the room because nobody else has gotten a word in. Buddy, you didn't "become more productive." You spent three weekends on a .vimrc so you could save four seconds renaming a variable, and you post your dotfiles repo like it's a baby picture. You remapped Caps Lock to Escape and now treat everyone else's keyboard like a character flaw. You say "I live in the terminal" like it's a lifestyle and not just where you got stuck. Your whole identity is a joke about not knowing how to quit, and honestly, you never learned. Here you are, still talking. You say "ciw" out loud at parties. You switched to Neovim just so you'd have something new to announce. And the payoff? You edit text exactly as fast as the rest of us, hands proudly on home row, with nobody watching.

b.text:
Vim. The only program where "how do I leave?" has more Stack Overflow views than most religions have followers. Two million people asked, and the answer was colon, q, exclamation point, which reads less like a command and more like a hostage's final words.

Vim stands for "Vi Improved." Improved from a 1976 terminal whose arrow keys were printed on H, J, K, and L. Fifty years later, Vim's still out here like, "Why fix what you can turn into a personality?"

You don't type in Vim. You type a sentence, then discover you deleted four lines, yanked a paragraph into register W, and started recording a macro.

Crash it once and it leaves a .swp file behind, like a ghost whispering, "Recover, Edit anyway, Quit, or Abort?"

Even its fans forked it. Neovim exists because Vim users wanted Vim, minus Vim.

facts: Nevada legalized casino gambling in 1931, the year construction of the Hoover Dam began nearby.
Most of the Strip lies not in the city of Las Vegas but in the unincorporated town of Paradise.
The Sphere, opened in 2023 at a cost of about $2.3 billion, is the largest spherical building in the world.
'What happens here, stays here' was launched by the local convention and visitors authority in 2003.
Lake Mead, its water source, fell in July 2022 to about 1,040 feet, its lowest since the reservoir first filled in 1937, and dropped below that mark again in August 2026.

a.text:
Las Vegas, the only city where you can see the Eiffel Tower, a pyramid, and Venice in one afternoon and still feel like you never left a strip mall in Ohio. You're a city built in the desert out of pure spite and borrowed water. The Colorado River is literally drying up so a fake volcano can erupt every fifteen minutes for a guy in cargo shorts holding a yard-long margarita.

Your casinos have no clocks and no windows, which is smart, because nobody wants to know it's 9 a.m. on a Tuesday and Grandma's on her third oxygen tank at the Wheel of Fortune slots.

"What happens in Vegas stays in Vegas"? Sure. Mostly your 401(k). And now you've got the Sphere, a giant glowing eyeball, so the whole city can watch you make every mistake in 4K.
