The joke is that the Sphere turns the city's famous secrecy slogan into a broadcast of its mistakes, which contradicts the "stays in Vegas" idea.

facts: Began in 1976 as a set of macros for the TECO editor at MIT's AI Lab, written by Richard Stallman and others; GNU Emacs followed in 1985.
Extensible in its own Lisp dialect, Emacs Lisp; the standing joke is that it is a fine operating system lacking only a good editor.
Ships with a psychotherapist (M-x doctor), Tetris, a mail client, a calendar, and a web browser (eww).
An old backronym is 'Eight Megabytes And Constantly Swapping', from when 8 MB was a lot of memory.
'Emacs pinky' is the name for the hand strain blamed on its Control-key chords.

a.text:
Emacs is the only text editor that ships with a psychotherapist, and you'll need it. M-x doctor exists because the developers knew exactly what they were doing to people.

It's a great operating system. It has a mail client, a web browser, Tetris, and a Lisp interpreter. What it lacks is a decent text editor. Its most beloved package is Evil mode, which is just Vim wearing an Emacs costume. That's like buying a Ferrari and installing a horse.

Want to save? C-x C-s. Want to quit? C-x C-c. Want to feel your left pinky again? Too late. Emacs stands for "Escape Meta Alt Control Shift," and the RSI stands for "you chose this."

Every user has a 4,000-line init.el they don't understand, copied from strangers on Stack Overflow in 2009.

b.text: Let's hear it for the people who live inside Emacs. They read email in mu4e, browse the web in eww, and get therapy from M-x doctor, the only therapist who'll put up with them. Their whole life is in org-mode: a 4,000-line to-do file where "fix init.el" has been a TODO since 2011. They don't use a computer; they negotiate with it in Lisp. Every problem gets solved by writing a function, and every function creates a new problem. They've declared init.el bankruptcy three times and still owe. Ask what they've built and they'll proudly show you a mode for managing their other modes. And the payoff? A pinky that clicks like a castanet from holding Control since the Clinton administration, and the quiet dignity of being the only person alive who knows how to leave. C-x C-c. They never do.

facts: Released to consumers in January 2007, after the 'Longhorn' project was reset in 2004 and headline features such as the WinFS file system were dropped.
User Account Control prompted so often that Apple's 'Get a Mac' campaign ran an ad about 'Cancel or Allow'.
'Windows Vista Capable' stickers went on PCs that could only run Home Basic, without the Aero interface, and led to a class-action lawsuit.
Windows 7 (2009), widely praised, was largely a tuned-up Vista on the same kernel line; Vista support ended in April 2017.

a.text: Let's hear it for the day-one Vista crowd, the people who lined up at CompUSA on January 30th, 2007 because a billboard said "The Wow Starts Now." You paid $399 for Ultimate so Flip 3D could shuffle the same three windows you used to Alt-Tab through. Your laptop had a "Vista Capable" sticker and 512 megs of RAM, which is like slapping "Marathon Capable" on a hamster. You wanted to look like the future; you had Aero turned off by Wednesday. Your printer quit. Your Sound Blaster went mute. Your "Ultimate Extras" turned out to be a poker game and a promise. And every time you tried to show off, the screen went dark and asked, "Are you sure?" Buddy, nobody was sure. Not even Microsoft. They were already working on Windows 7.

b.text:
Windows Vista, everybody! Microsoft spent five years building you as "Longhorn," and somehow you still came out premature.

Your slogan was "The Wow Starts Now." You meant "Now" as in "after the loading circle finishes." People bought laptops with "Vista Capable" stickers, which turned out to mean "capable of being sued over." Those machines couldn't even run Aero, so they got a see-through window theme with nothing to see.

And User Account Control! You asked "Are you sure?" so many times that you became the first operating system with separation anxiety.

You came in six editions, including "Ultimate," whose big exclusive was DreamScene: a moving wallpaper for the ten minutes you weren't hunting for printer drivers.

Microsoft had to trick people into liking you. The Mojave Experiment! Your own parents had to put you in disguise.

Your greatest feature? The XP downgrade.

facts: Chosen as a compromise because neither Sydney nor Melbourne would accept the other as capital; Australia's constitution required the capital to be at least 100 miles from Sydney.
Designed by the Chicago architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin, who won an international competition in 1912.
Its centrepiece, Lake Burley Griffin, is artificial, created by damming the Molonglo River in 1963-64.
Parliament House (1988) is built into Capital Hill under a lawn meant for citizens to walk over their politicians; the lawn was fenced off in 2017 for security.
Melbourne served as the capital until 1927 while Canberra was being built.

a.text: You moved to Canberra for the job. Brave. You looked at Sydney rents, did the maths, and decided your personality was negotiable. Now you're an EL1 who says "stakeholder" at barbecues and talks about Senate Estimates like a war you survived. Your lanyard has a richer social life than you do. You promised your Melbourne friends a visit; they've cancelled twice for weddings in Bali. You've developed opinions about Gungahlin. Your wild Saturday is Braddon brunch, followed by complaining it was "basically Sydney prices." And what did it get you? A secure job, a three-bedroom in Tuggeranong, and a security clearance confirming the government checked thoroughly and found nothing interesting. You came for two years. That was 2009. Your kid now says "on the Hill" unprompted, and you've never been prouder or more quietly trapped.

b.text:
Canberra exists because Sydney and Melbourne couldn't agree on anything, so they built a city that nobody could possibly be jealous of. Mission accomplished.

It was designed by an American architect, which explains why it feels like a very nice airport with sheep. The roundabouts are so plentiful that locals don't give directions, they give revolutions. The lake is fake, the population is mostly public servants waiting for Friday, and the kangaroos outnumber the nightlife.

Your Parliament House is literally buried in a hill so people can walk on the roof, the only time Australians get to stand on politicians.

For your centenary you commissioned the Skywhale, a giant flying balloon with ten enormous boobs, and somehow that's still the most exciting thing to happen here.

Canberra: home of Summernats, Floriade, and legally purchasable X-rated videos. Burnouts, tulips and porn, because you've got to do something until the next Senate estimates hearing.

facts: The same polymer as Plexiglas and acrylic glass, dissolved in anisole or chlorobenzene and spun into a thin film.
The oldest electron-beam resist still in everyday use; IBM researchers reported it as one in the late 1960s.
Positive tone: the beam breaks polymer chains and the exposed region dissolves in a MIBK:IPA developer.
Resolves below 10 nm but has poor sensitivity, so doses of hundreds to over a thousand µC/cm² (depending on voltage) make writing slow.
Poor dry-etch resistance, so it is used mostly for lift-off rather than as an etch mask.

a.text: PMMA, you're the same plastic as a hockey rink window, and somehow that's your most dignified job. You've been "high resolution" since the 1970s, which is like bragging about your SAT score at your retirement party. Sure, you'll resolve sub-10-nanometer lines, if someone stands there blasting you with electrons for an eternity. Your sensitivity is so low the beam current has gotten tenure. You don't even develop properly without MIBK and IPA holding your hand in a one-to-three ratio. And your whole personality is chain scission: you literally fall apart when someone pays attention to you. Then hit you with too much dose and you crosslink and flip to negative tone, a full identity crisis. And dry etch? You melt in plasma faster than an ice sculpture at a barbecue. Honestly, the only thing you're consistently good at is lift-off: leaving.

b.text: You still spin PMMA. Of course you do. Your advisor's thesis used it, his advisor's thesis used it, and somewhere a 1970s IBM engineer remains the most cutting-edge person in your academic lineage. You call it "high resolution" the way your uncle calls his Camry "reliable." You book the e-beam overnight because your dose is measured in geological time, then dunk your chip in MIBK:IPA with a stopwatch and a prayer, chilling the developer like it's a fine Riesling. When the plasma etch eats your mask before your substrate, you just whisper "bilayer, 495K under 950K" like it's a personality. You're not chasing nanostructures. You're chasing a recipe nobody can blame you for. And it works: the gold lifted off beautifully. Your career is still soaking in acetone, waiting for something to come loose.

facts: A Portuguese settlement from the 1550s until the handover to China in December 1999.
Casino revenue passed the Las Vegas Strip's in 2006, and at its 2013 peak, about $45 billion, was roughly seven times the Strip's.
One company, STDM, held the casino monopoly for four decades until licences opened to competition in 2002.
Among the most densely populated places on Earth, at roughly 20,000 people per square kilometre.
The Cotai Strip stands on land reclaimed from the sea between the islands of Taipa and Coloane.

a.text: You lost it on Hong Kong stocks, so you took the TurboJET to win it back, because nothing says "financial plan" like a ferry with a cancellation policy. You're the guy at the Grand Lisboa squeezing a baccarat card like it owes you rent, blowing on it, peeling the corner so slowly the dealer ages. Red underwear, three days unwashed, "for luck." Baccarat is a coin flip and you've built a religion around it. You told your wife it's a work trip, and technically your work now is the pawn shop next door, which buys Rolexes faster than you can say "one more shoe." By hour nine you're eating an egg tart for dinner and calling it Portuguese culture. You came to win it all back. You leave by bus over the bridge with no luck, no Rolex, and a watch tan.

b.text: Macau, you're the only place where the most famous church is just a wall. The Ruins of St. Paul's: a gorgeous front with absolutely nothing behind it, which is basically your whole personality. You've got a fake Venice with a painted sky, a fake Paris with a half-size Eiffel Tower, and you're so tiny you had to dump dirt into the ocean just to fit a runway. You out-earned Las Vegas several times over, and your signature dish is still a pork chop jammed in a bun. The Portuguese stayed four hundred years and left you an egg tart and street signs nobody reads. The Grand Lisboa looks like a golden pineapple having a breakdown. And the Macau Tower's big attraction is jumping off it, which, after a night at the baccarat tables, is less a thrill ride and more a financial plan.

facts: Hydrogen silsesquioxane, sold by Dow Corning as FOx ('flowable oxide') and designed as a spin-on dielectric for chip interconnects; lithographers adopted it as a negative-tone resist.
Exposure converts its cage structure into a cross-linked, silica-like network, so the developed pattern is essentially SiO2.
Holds the resolution records for electron-beam lithography: isolated features around 5 nm, dense lines below 10 nm half-pitch, with high-contrast 'salty' NaOH/NaCl development.

Must be kept refrigerated (Dow Corning's datasheet gives a six-month shelf life at 5 °C); the solution ages into a jelly, and its effective sensitivity shifts with processing delays because cross-linking continues after exposure.

DuPont, which inherited Dow Corning's FOx/XR-1541 HSQ line, discontinued it and ended production at the end of 2025; labs such as EPFL's CMi switched to third-party HSQ from EM Resist or DisChem, both formulated from AQM powder.

a.text: So you switched to HSQ for the resolution. Bold move for someone whose devices still die at wire bonding. You saw one SEM of 6-nanometer lines at a conference and decided PMMA was beneath you. Now you're writing at a dose so high your name sits on the e-beam calendar like a hostage note. Your resist lives in the fridge next to somebody's yogurt, and you check its age more often than your own. You develop in salt water now, the closest you've come to a beach in three years. And congratulations on those gorgeous lines. They're basically glass, so the only way to fix a mistake is HF, a fume hood, and a long call to your mother. All this for one inset figure the reviewer will ask you to make bigger.

b.text:
HSQ, everybody! The only resist that ages faster than the grad student using it. You spin it Monday, expose it Tuesday, and suddenly your dose curve has gone through a midlife crisis. It has to live in the fridge like expired yogurt, and it's about as forgiving.

HSQ brags about sub-10-nanometer lines. Sure, if you've got six hours of write time, because this diva needs a dose that could sterilize a hospital. Then you develop it in TMAH, or, if you're desperate, *salt water*. Your whole career is literally seasoned with tears now.

And once it's exposed? It turns into glass. Brittle, cracking glass. You wanted a mask; you got a window that shatters when you look at it. Want it gone? Hope you enjoy hydrofluoric acid, the chemical that dissolves your bones.

HSQ: beautiful resolution, terrible personality. It's not negative-tone. It's just negative.

facts: California grows about 80% of the world's almonds.
A single almond takes about 1.1 US gallons (roughly 4 litres) of water to grow, a figure Mother Jones published in 2014 that spread during California's drought.

A 2015 US class action alleged Almond Breeze contained only about 2% almonds; it partly survived a motion to dismiss, was stayed in 2017 pending a separate Blue Diamond labelling settlement, and the plaintiffs then dropped it.
Pollinating California's almond orchards each February requires trucking in most of the commercial honeybee colonies in the United States.
Medieval European cooks used almond milk as a Lenten substitute for dairy, centuries before the current fashion.

a.text:
Almond milk, you're the only drink that needs a lawyer to defend its name. The dairy industry sued because, technically, nobody has ever milked an almond. We looked. No nipples.

You're about two percent almonds. The rest is water, gellan gum, and confidence. You're not milk. You're a nut that got waterboarded and called it wellness.

And speaking of water: it takes over a gallon to grow a single almond. California is in a drought so you can be beige in a latte. Bees get trucked across the country like seasonal laborers just to make you, and a lot of them don't come home.

Leave you in the fridge for two days and you separate like you're ashamed of yourself. Fair. I'd need to be shaken too if I cost seven dollars and tasted like a wet sympathy card.

b.text:
You switched to almond milk to save the planet. Bold move, picking the one crop that drinks California like it's an open bar. Every latte you order, a farmer in the Central Valley watches his well go dry and thinks, "At least Kayleigh's being sustainable."

And you didn't save a cow. You just outsourced the suffering to bees, trucked cross-country every February to work themselves to death in an orchard, while you post about dairy being cruel.

You're not after a healthier Earth. You're after the barista hearing you say it. That little pause before "almond, please" is the biggest environmental impact you've ever had.

And now the oat milk people look at you the way you used to look at skim drinkers. You picked a side in the milk war, and you lost.

facts: Spun out in 2013 from the internal chat tool of Tiny Speck's failed game Glitch; founder Stewart Butterfield had earlier spun Flickr out of another failed game.
The name is a backronym: 'Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge'.
Salesforce bought it for $27.7 billion in 2021.
Filed an EU antitrust complaint against Microsoft in 2020 over the bundling of Teams with Office.

a.text:
Let's hear it for the founders running a company on Slack. You wanted a culture of transparency. You got 340 public channels and every real decision happening in a DM called "quick q."

You don't manage people anymore. You manage a green dot. You jiggle your mouse at your kid's birthday party so the team knows you're "around." Your entire leadership style is the eyes emoji. Someone asks for budget approval, you react with a little thumbs-up, and three weeks later legal wants to know what the thumbs-up meant. Nobody knows. It was legally binding and spiritually ambiguous.

And when something truly matters? You type "hey" and walk away. Just "hey." That's not a message, that's a hostage situation.

You promised Slack would kill meetings. Instead you invented the huddle: a meeting that ambushes people while they're eating.

b.text:
Slack. Named after the one thing you'll never have again.

You promised to kill email, and you did, by replacing it with forty channels that are each email with a typing indicator. Nothing builds dread like "Greg is typing..." for ninety seconds, followed by "hey." Just "hey." Greg, that's not a message, that's a hostage situation.

You gave us threads, so every conversation happens in two places and nobody knows which one's real. You gave us huddles: a meeting that jumps out of a bush. You gave us the green dot, so my boss can monitor my bathroom breaks like a heart rate.

And that knock sound. I hear it in the grocery store. I hear it at funerals.

Slack, you're the only app that needs three gigs of RAM to tell me someone reacted with a dancing parrot.

facts: Launched in 2017, bundled at no extra charge into Office 365, and replaced Skype for Business.
After Slack's antitrust complaint, Microsoft unbundled Teams from Office in the EU in 2023 and worldwide in 2024; the European Commission still sent a statement of objections in 2024.
Microsoft reported 320 million monthly active users in 2023.
Microsoft shut down consumer Skype in May 2025 and sent its users to Teams.

a.text:
Let's hear it for the IT director who chose Microsoft Teams, a man who has never once chosen anything. It came bundled with Outlook, like coleslaw you're contractually obligated to eat. The EU had to force Microsoft to stop shoving it on people, and your company still went back for seconds. The whole pitch was "It's already in the license." So was Clippy, Gary.

Management loves it because now they can watch your little dot. Green means productive. Yellow means you went to the bathroom and Linda noticed. They didn't want collaboration. They wanted a heart monitor.

And what did it get them? Every meeting opens with eight adults asking "Can you see my screen?" while a VP uses the raise-hand button to interrupt people *harder*. Congratulations: you saved nine dollars a seat and lost the will to live.

b.text: Microsoft Teams is the only app that got popular the way a parking ticket gets popular: it came free with Office 365 and nobody could say no. It's a chat app that eats more RAM than Chrome, which is like a goldfish outeating a horse. It marks you "Away" if you blink for five minutes, which is why half of corporate America owns a mouse jiggler. Every file you share vanishes into SharePoint, a place so mysterious even Microsoft sends search parties. There's chat, there's channels, there's "posts," and nobody knows which one Kevin used. They released "New Teams" to replace "Classic Teams," and somehow both are running on my laptop right now, fighting. And that notification sound? That little knock-knock haunts people on vacation. Teams, you didn't win the remote work war. You were just pre-installed.

facts: Leslie Lamport wrote LaTeX in the early 1980s and released it in 1984 as a macro layer on Donald Knuth's TeX (1978), which Knuth built because he disliked how the galley proofs of the new edition of his own book looked.

TeX's version number converges on π (3.141592653 since 2021), and Knuth's TeX bug bounty started at one hexadecimal dollar, $2.56, doubling yearly until frozen at $327.68; he stopped mailing real cheques in 2008 after fraud and now credits accounts at his fictional Bank of San Serriffe, and only 9 of the 275 cheques he sent from 2006 on were ever cashed.

Its best-known warning is 'Underfull \hbox (badness 10000)'; overfull lines are reported as 'Overfull \hbox (Npt too wide)', and figures float to wherever the algorithm decides, not where the author put them.
A single missing brace can produce an error reported pages away from the mistake, and a document can need three compiler passes to get its references right.

a.text: LaTeX, you're the only software that makes PhDs feel stupid. You're from 1984 and you dress like it: backslashes everywhere, curly braces like a nervous tic. I tell you to put a figure "here," and you treat "here" as a suggestion, then file it four pages later next to the bibliography, like a sock lost in a dryer. Your error messages are poetry: "Missing $ inserted." Inserted where? Why? You won't say. You just blame line 1 of a 40-page file because I typed an underscore in a URL. My citations are double question marks until I compile you twice, then a third time, out of spite. And everyone needs to know it's pronounced "lay-tech," not like the glove. Honestly, at least the glove stretches. Overfull \hbox? Badness 10000? Buddy, that's not a warning. That's your autobiography.

b.text: Let's talk about the guy who writes a two-page memo in LaTeX. Your memo is about the break room fridge, but it's in Computer Modern, so everyone reads it expecting it to end with a theorem. "Fridge Policy, Section 1.1." Buddy, there's no Section 1.2. You spent forty minutes on a preamble longer than the memo. Twelve \usepackage lines to say "label your yogurt." You compiled it three times because the cross-reference said "see Section ??" on page one, referencing page one. You're not after clarity. You're after someone asking, "Is this LaTeX?" so you can say "Oh, habit," like a man who still mentions his thesis at parties. And it gets you exactly one thing: a PDF nobody can edit, so when Karen fixes a typo, she retypes the whole thing in Word.

facts: Launched in 2017, bundled at no extra charge into Office 365, and replaced Skype for Business.
After Slack's antitrust complaint, Microsoft unbundled Teams from Office in the EU in 2023 and worldwide in 2024; the European Commission still sent a statement of objections in 2024.
Microsoft reported 320 million monthly active users in 2023.
Microsoft shut down consumer Skype in May 2025 and sent its users to Teams.

a.text:
Let's hear it for the CIO who chose Microsoft Teams, a decision made the way you pick ketchup packets: it came free with the order. Nobody evaluated it. It showed up inside the Office 365 license like a toy in a cereal box, and this man stood up at the all-hands and called it a "collaboration strategy." Sir, the European Commission had to force Microsoft to unbundle it. You lost a negotiation to a checkbox.

And what did he really want? The little status dot. He doesn't read your work; he reads your color. Go yellow after five minutes of actual thinking and you're on a list. Congratulations: you saved forty grand on Slack and spent it all on adults jiggling their mouse like raccoons on a treadmill. Your files are lost somewhere in SharePoint, and your morale is permanently "Away."

b.text:
Microsoft Teams is the only app that marks me "Away" after five minutes of deep thought but keeps me "Available" for three hours after I've died. It's not software. It's a hall monitor in a purple vest.

Teams eats more RAM than the game I'm pretending not to play. It launches on startup uninvited, then takes four minutes to load a chat that just says "ok."

Where are my files? SharePoint. Where's SharePoint? Nobody knows. Teams ships them off like a kid to boarding school.

Then they gave us "New Teams," which is Old Teams with a fresh coat of lag. IT has told me to "clear the cache" so often I do it in my sleep.

Nobody chose Teams. It came free with Office. Fitting, since so did Clippy.

facts: Reported by Sumio Iijima in Nature in 1991.
Promised as the cable for a space elevator; a 2006 analysis showed that ordinary defects cut the strength of a macroscopic cable far below the ideal value.
Long, rigid multi-walled nanotubes behaved like asbestos fibres in a 2008 mouse study in Nature Nanotechnology.
Sorting metallic from semiconducting tubes has blocked nanotube electronics for three decades; MIT's 16-bit RV16X-NANO processor (2019) is still a lab demonstration.
Today they are sold mainly as a conductive additive in lithium-ion battery electrodes.

a.text: Nanotube founders are the only people who've said "within five years" every year since 1991 and kept a straight face. They open with a slide of a space elevator, then ask for seed money to make a vial of black dust. Every deck has the same line, "a hundred times stronger than steel," and every deck is quietly a plan to sell additive to tennis racket companies. These are PhDs who spent six years sorting chirality and came out wanting a Tesla. The pitch is always "we've solved scale," and the demo is always one centimeter long. VCs keep a nanotube guy around like a lucky rabbit's foot: he never pays off, but he makes the fund sound visionary. And when someone asks about lung toxicity, he says "totally different from asbestos" with the confidence of a man who googled it in the elevator. The regular one.

b.text:
Carbon nanotubes, everybody! The only material that's been "five years away" since 1991. You're a hundred times stronger than steel, and you've used that strength to hold together... a tennis racket. They promised us a space elevator; you can't get past a few centimeters without a defect. That's not a cable, that's a toothpick with a press agent.

You're basically graphene that rolled itself up out of insecurity, and graphene still got the Nobel. Your cousin the buckyball got one too. You got a shoutout in a bike-frame brochure.

You can't even decide if you're a metal or a semiconductor; it depends on the angle you got rolled at. You clump together like nerds at a mixer, and the second you escape, you lodge in lungs like asbestos. Strongest thing on Earth, and your best trick is ending up in a safety data sheet.

facts: Inaugurated on 21 April 1960 after about 41 months of construction, moving the capital inland from Rio de Janeiro.
Lúcio Costa's Plano Piloto is laid out like an airplane (or a bird, or a cross), with Oscar Niemeyer's government buildings along the fuselage.
Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987, less than 30 years after it was built.
Planned for 500,000 residents; the Federal District now has about 3 million, most in satellite towns outside the plan.
Built for the car: wide avenues, few pedestrian crossings, and distances that make walking impractical.

a.text: Brasília, you're what happens when an architect gets an entire country's budget and nobody says, "Maybe add a sidewalk?" You're shaped like an airplane, which is fitting, because everyone's goal is to board one by Friday afternoon. Your addresses read like Wi-Fi passwords: "SQS 308, Bloco C, apartamento 402." That's not a home. That's a parking spot on a spaceship. Kubitschek promised "fifty years in five," and you delivered: it's been sixty-five years and you still feel unfinished. Your Congress has one bowl facing up to receive the money and one facing down to hide it. You've got a row of identical ministry buildings so nobody can tell which one the scandal came from. In August the humidity drops so low that the only thing drier than the air is a deputy's sense of shame. Even your lake is fake. Honestly? On brand.

b.text: Walking in Brasília is for three kinds of people: tourists who saw the Esplanada on a postcard and thought "that looks close," architecture students who love Niemeyer from a safe distance, and the guy whose car is in the shop. You're not a pedestrian. You're an ant that wandered onto a blueprint. You want bread? The padaria is "right there" across the Eixão, so you sprint six lanes like you owe the government money. Which, let's be honest, is also your employer. Your sneakers are permanently red from the dirt trails carved by every other fool who refused to walk around a tesourinha. And on Sunday, when they close the Eixão, you finally stroll down the middle of the highway like a man who's won something. You haven't. Everyone else just stopped driving for one day.

facts: Invented in 1962 by Sam Panopoulos, a Greek immigrant, at the Satellite Restaurant in Chatham, Ontario, Canada; named after the brand of canned pineapple he used.
Iceland's president Guðni Th. Jóhannesson said in 2017 that he would ban pineapple on pizza if he could, then clarified that a president has no such power.

Hawaii is no longer a major pineapple producer: Del Monte shut its Hawaiian pineapple operations in November 2006, two years ahead of its announced 2008 exit, the state's last cannery closed in 2007, and most canned pineapple now comes from Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines.
Panopoulos, whose restaurant also served Chinese dishes, told the Toronto Sun in 2010 that 'in those days people didn't mix the tastes like sweet and sour, except for Chinese food'.

a.text:
Hawaiian pizza. Let's start with the name, because that's the first lie. You were invented in Ontario. By a Greek guy. In 1962. You're Hawaiian the way a tiki bar in Ohio is Hawaiian. The only tropical thing about you is the can your pineapple came out of.

And that pineapple: warm, wet, weeping syrup into the crust until the middle slice folds like a lawn chair. Pineapple contains an enzyme that breaks down protein, so the fruit is literally trying to digest the ham. Even your toppings hate each other.

And the ham! Not prosciutto, not even pepperoni. Just pale pink squares that look like they were chiseled out of a deli's floor tile.

You're the pizza people order to seem quirky. "I'm so random!" No, Kevin. That's a fruit cup that fell on a pizza, and nobody cleaned it up.

b.text:
People who order Hawaiian pizza want you to know they're brave. They say "I know, I know" before anyone has said a word, because for them the pineapple isn't a topping, it's a personality. This is a person whose entire rebellious phase fits in a box for $14.99. They've never gotten a tattoo, never quit a job, never sent food back, but once a month they look a teenage cashier dead in the eye and say "pineapple" like they're defusing a bomb.

And they always want to split one with you. Half Hawaiian, half "normal." That's not a compromise. That's a hostage negotiation.

Best part? It isn't even Hawaiian. A Greek guy invented it in Ontario. So congratulations: your one act of rebellion is a Canadian pretending he's on vacation.

facts: Nevada legalized casino gambling in 1931, the year construction of the Hoover Dam began nearby.
Most of the Strip lies not in the city of Las Vegas but in the unincorporated town of Paradise.
The Sphere, opened in 2023 at a cost of about $2.3 billion, is the largest spherical building in the world.
'What happens here, stays here' was launched by the local convention and visitors authority in 2003.
Lake Mead, its water source, fell in July 2022 to about 1,040 feet, its lowest since the reservoir first filled in 1937, and dropped below that mark again in August 2026.

a.text:
Las Vegas, the only city that looked at the Mojave Desert and said, "You know what this needs? Venice." Nothing says Italian romance like a gondolier singing in a mall next to a Cheesecake Factory.

You built a half-size Eiffel Tower, a fake New York, and a pyramid, because why visit the world when you can visit its gift shop?

No clocks, no windows, and carpet designed by a migraine, all so you won't notice you've been feeding a penny slot since Tuesday.

"What happens in Vegas stays in Vegas." Yeah. Especially your money. And the $45 resort fee for a pool you couldn't use because a bachelor party from Ohio was in it.

And Lake Mead's drying up so fast they keep finding bodies. Even the mob's secrets can't stay in Vegas anymore.

b.text:
You flew Spirit to Las Vegas to get rich. Sit with that. You paid extra for a carry-on and called it an investment strategy. You've got a blackjack "system" from a YouTube guy filming in his mom's kitchen. You told your wife it's "basically math." Sure. So is a second mortgage.

Here's what you won: a Caesars Rewards card, a "free" buffet you earned by losing eleven hundred dollars, and a room "upgrade" overlooking the Bellagio parking structure. You hit four hundred bucks on a Wheel of Fortune slot at 4 a.m. and fed it right back like it owed you child support.

The pit boss knows your name. That's not respect, that's inventory.

And you'll fly home saying "I basically broke even," which is Vegas for "Please don't check the joint account."

facts: California grows about 80% of the world's almonds.
A single almond takes about 1.1 US gallons (roughly 4 litres) of water to grow, a figure Mother Jones published in 2014 that spread during California's drought.

A 2015 US class action alleged Almond Breeze contained only about 2% almonds; it partly survived a motion to dismiss, was stayed in 2017 pending a separate Blue Diamond labelling settlement, and the plaintiffs then dropped it.
Pollinating California's almond orchards each February requires trucking in most of the commercial honeybee colonies in the United States.
Medieval European cooks used almond milk as a Lenten substitute for dairy, centuries before the current fashion.

a.text: Let's hear it for the people who switched to almond milk to save the planet. You watched one documentary about cow farts and panicked straight into the arms of a nut that needs a gallon of water apiece. Congratulations: you fled methane and landed on drought. California is cracking like a crème brûlée, and you're out here draining a Central Valley aquifer because you can't make eye contact with a Holstein. And the bees! Billions of them trucked across the country on semis, dying by the hive, so you can tell a coworker you "don't really do dairy." That's not environmentalism. That's relocating the crime scene. You didn't save the Earth. You just moved the guilt somewhere sunnier, slapped a leaf on it, and paid an eighty-cent upcharge for the privilege of feeling better about it.

b.text:
Almond milk, you're the only drink that needs a lawyer to defend its name. The dairy industry sued because, technically, nobody has ever milked an almond. We looked. No nipples.

You're about two percent almonds. The rest is water, gellan gum, and confidence. You're not milk. You're a nut that got waterboarded and called it wellness.

And speaking of water: it takes over a gallon to grow a single almond. California is in a drought so you can be beige in a latte. Bees get trucked across the country like seasonal laborers just to make you, and a lot of them don't come home.

Leave you in the fridge for two days and you separate like you're ashamed of yourself. Fair. I'd need to be shaken too if I cost seven dollars and tasted like a wet sympathy card.

facts: Released in February 2024 at $3,499, with an external battery pack on a cable rated for about two hours.
'EyeSight' shows a rendering of the wearer's eyes on an outward-facing screen.
Apple calls it 'spatial computing' and its App Store rules tell developers not to describe apps as AR, VR, XR, or MR.
Reports during 2024 said Apple had cut production; analysts' first-year sales estimates were well under a million units.
Weighs 600-650 g, before the battery.

a.text: Look at this guy on the F train, pinching at nothing like he's seasoning a ghost. He spent thirty-five hundred dollars to ride the subway on the surface of the moon, and the moon still smells like pee. He cranked the Digital Crown all the way to Joshua Tree, and the mariachi band found him anyway. That's the dream: rich enough to be somewhere else, broke enough to still be on the F. And he *wants* you to notice. That's why his fake cartoon eyes glow on the outside, so strangers know he's "present." Buddy, nobody's checking. You're on Mount Hood. He gets two hours of battery and three stops of dignity, with a cable snaking into his pocket like a subway IV drip. Meanwhile, the guy next to him reading an actual book? That guy's already somewhere else, for free.

b.text:
Apple Vision Pro, you cost $3,499 and still need a battery on a cord like a 1996 Walkman. Two hours of charge? That's not spatial computing, that's a matinee. Wear glasses? Zeiss inserts, extra. Apple saw you squinting and smelled revenue.

And EyeSight! A front screen showing your eyes so people feel connected. Nothing says "I'm present" like blurry cartoon eyeballs trapped behind ski-goggle glass. Your Persona avatar looks like a hostage video directed by a ghost.

You promised the future, and Netflix wouldn't even make you an app. You strap over a pound to dads' faces so they can record "spatial memories" of birthdays they watched through a screen.

Apple said you'd never see the world the same way. True. Now it's through a $3,500 face fridge.

facts: Has been 'about 30 years away' since the 1950s; at the 1955 Geneva atoms-for-peace conference, Homi Bhabha predicted fusion power within two decades.
ITER, agreed in 2006 for first plasma in 2016, re-baselined in 2024 to start research operations in 2034 and deuterium-tritium burning in 2039, at a cost estimated above €20 billion.
NIF's December 2022 'ignition' shot released 3.15 MJ from 2.05 MJ of laser energy; the lasers drew about 300 MJ from the grid to fire.
Private fusion companies had raised more than $7 billion by 2024.

a.text:
Nuclear fusion, everybody! The only energy source that's been thirty years away for seventy years. You're not the future, you're a toddler promising to clean his room after the next funding cycle.

You heat plasma to 150 million degrees, ten times hotter than the core of the sun, and still can't do what the sun does for free while being a ball of gas with no PhD.

ITER started at five billion euros. It's now north of twenty, and it hasn't produced a watt. That's not a reactor, that's a French timeshare.

In 2022 you finally got "net energy gain" by ignoring the 300 megajoules the lasers pulled from the wall. That's like saying your restaurant's profitable if you don't count rent.

And your solution to fuel shortages is mining helium-3 on the moon. Buddy, you can't even make it to Tuesday.

b.text: Let's hear it for the fusion people, the only scientists who've been "ten years away" since my grandfather had hair. You can hold plasma hotter than the sun for a few seconds, but you can't hold a deadline for one decade. Every press release: "Net energy gain!" Sure, if you don't count the electricity bill for the lasers. That's like me saying I'm profitable if you ignore rent. ITER got approved when Myspace was cool, and it's still assembling the donut. And the startups: "We're different, we have venture capital." Great, now the sun is ten years away *and* has a pitch deck. Honestly, it's a beautiful racket: promise infinite clean energy, collect the grant, retire before anyone plugs in a toaster. You're not building a star. You're building a pension.

facts: First shipped for the Macintosh in 1985; the Windows version followed in 1987.

Silently converts gene names such as SEPT2 and MARCH1 into dates; by August 2020 the HUGO Gene Nomenclature Committee had renamed 27 human genes (MARCH1 became MARCHF1, SEPT2 became SEPTIN2) and published guidelines in Nature Genetics to stop it.
In October 2020, Public Health England lost 15,841 COVID-19 cases when a legacy .xls file hit its 65,536-row limit.
Reinhart and Rogoff's 2010 paper 'Growth in a Time of Debt', cited for austerity policies, omitted five countries through a spreadsheet range error found by a graduate student in 2013.
Sheets have been capped at 1,048,576 rows by 16,384 columns since Excel 2007.

a.text: Excel, you're the only software that forced geneticists to rename human genes because you kept turning MARCH1 into March 1st. Scientists can edit DNA, but they couldn't edit you. You still think 1900 was a leap year. You've known it wasn't for forty years. You just don't care. You see a zip code like 02134 and go, "Leading zero? Not on my watch." You lost sixteen thousand UK COVID cases by quietly stopping at row 65,536. Your error messages are pure poetry: #REF!, #N/A, #VALUE!, and my favorite, a column of hashtags that just means "make me wider." And VLOOKUP: insert one column and the whole finance department enters witness protection. You're not a spreadsheet. You're a hostage situation with gridlines.

b.text: You run a company on Excel. Let's be clear about who you are: a guy who thinks "enterprise software" is a scam and "Q3_Forecast_FINAL_v9_USE_THIS_ONE.xlsx" is a system. You wanted control. You got Dave. Dave wrote a macro in 2014, and now Dave can never leave, die, or take a vacation, because payroll is a VLOOKUP only he understands. Your entire supply chain is one #REF! away from bankruptcy. You can't onboard a customer because the file is "locked for editing by Karen," and Karen is at lunch. You saved forty grand a year on a real database and lost it all the day someone sorted column B without column C. Your org chart is merged cells. Your audit trail is yellow and slightly different yellow. And your growth strategy has a hard ceiling: 1,048,576 rows.

facts: Oatly started in Sweden in the 1990s, built on Lund University research by Rickard Öste on lactose intolerance.
Oatly's slogan 'It's like milk but made for humans' was banned in Sweden in 2015 after the dairy lobby LRF Mjölk sued; Oatly then published the lawsuit as advertising.
Oatly listed on Nasdaq in May 2021 at a valuation near $10 billion; the shares later lost more than 90% of their value.

Commercial oat milk is made by breaking oat starch into maltose with amylase enzymes, and many brands, Oatly among them, add rapeseed oil; the result has more sugar and a higher glycaemic index than almond or soy milk.

a.text:
Oat milk, I want to say this as gently as I can, and I'll admit that gentleness isn't really my strong suit, but you are porridge that got a publicist. I'm not entirely sure how that happened, and I suppose nobody fully understands the chain of events that led here. Somebody looked at the breakfast of Victorian orphans and said, "What if it cost six dollars and had a font?" Honestly, that seems like the kind of idea that gets made in a meeting, approved by people who were probably pleased with themselves, and then shipped to grocery stores without anyone stopping to ask whether it should be.

Your carton talks to me. I didn't ask it to, and I'd like that on the record, although I realize nobody is keeping a record here. Oatly, I'm trying to make coffee, not get into a pen-pal situation with a beverage that writes like a substitute teacher who wants to be called "Dave." I just want to pour something into my mug, stir it, and get on with my morning, and instead I'm reading a little paragraph about the farmers and the planet and my own feelings. It's a lot to take in before 7 a.m., if I'm being completely honest with you.

Let's talk about what's actually in you, because the list is short and somewhat sobering. You're oats, water, and rapeseed oil. That's not milk, to be fair, or at least it isn't what I'd call milk in any ordinary sense. That's a salad dressing that gave up, which is about as close as I can get to describing it without sounding like I've lost my patience entirely. And to make matters a little worse, they had to add enzymes to turn your starch into sugar so you'd taste like something. In other words, the flavor isn't really coming from you so much as from a process that had to be arranged on your behalf. You're the only "health drink" that spikes my blood sugar like a Pop-Tart, which is a claim I wouldn't have believed had I not experienced it myself, more than once, usually before noon.

There's a "Barista Edition" now. Oat milk, there are two editions of you. I'll just say it plainly, since it seems like the sort of thing that needs saying plainly: two editions. Moby-Dick has fewer editions than you. That's a novel about a whale that took the author years to finish, and it has fewer versions than a carton of oat milk that was, as far as I can tell, invented last week and immediately given a sequel.

And you're beige. You make every latte look like dishwater with ambition. I don't say that to be cruel, or at least not only to be cruel. It's more that I've looked at the result many times, and the color is what it is, and no amount of foam art or clever branding seems to change what's sitting in the cup in front of me. The ambition is there, I'll grant you that, but it's the dishwater that wins the argument every single time.

Horses eat oats for free, and they still look embarrassed for us. I think that's the most accurate thing anyone has said about this whole situation, and I'm sorry if that sounds like an overstatement, though I doubt the horses would disagree.

b.text:
Oat milk, you are porridge that got a publicist. Somebody looked at the breakfast of Victorian orphans and said, "What if it cost six dollars and had a font?"

Your carton talks to me. Oatly, I'm trying to make coffee, not get into a pen-pal situation with a beverage that writes like a substitute teacher who wants to be called "Dave."

You're oats, water, and rapeseed oil. That's not milk, that's a salad dressing that gave up. And they had to add enzymes to turn your starch into sugar so you'd taste like something. You're the only "health drink" that spikes my blood sugar like a Pop-Tart.

There's a "Barista Edition" now. Oat milk, there are two editions of you. Moby-Dick has fewer editions than you.

And you're beige. You make every latte look like dishwater with ambition.

Horses eat oats for free, and they still look embarrassed for us.

facts: A Wi-Fi-connected cold-press juicer launched in 2016 at $699, later cut to $399, that squeezed proprietary bags of chopped produce sold by subscription.
Raised about $120 million from investors including Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins.
In April 2017, Bloomberg reporters squeezed the packs by hand and got 7.5 ounces of juice in 90 seconds, faster than the machine's 8 ounces in about two minutes.
Each pack carried a QR code that the press scanned and checked online before squeezing; it refused expired packs and would not run at all unless connected to Wi-Fi.
Shut down in September 2017 and offered refunds on the machine.

a.text:
Juicero, you beautiful $120 million monument to Silicon Valley. You launched at seven hundred dollars to squeeze a bag. A bag! Then Bloomberg reporters squeezed that same bag with their bare hands and got basically the same juice, only faster. You got outperformed by a guy with a grip strength of "typing."

Doug Evans bragged you pressed with four tons of force, enough to lift two Teslas. Buddy, it's kale. The kale didn't need a forklift.

And it needed Wi-Fi. It scanned a QR code before it'd let you drink. Your router goes down and suddenly your breakfast is asking for credentials. Who designs a juicer that can be bricked?

Google Ventures funded this. Kleiner Perkins funded this. Somewhere, a man is still holding a lukewarm pouch, waiting for a firmware update so he's allowed to eat a carrot.

b.text: You paid four hundred dollars so a startup could check your juice's expiration date over Wi-Fi. That's not wellness. That's asking a server for permission to have breakfast. These are people who looked at a bag of chopped kale and thought, "This needs a subscription." People who wanted to be someone who juices without ever touching a fruit. Then Bloomberg showed the whole world you could squeeze the pack with your bare hands. Faster. For free. Your grandmother has been doing that with a lemon since 1952. You didn't buy a juicer; you bought the privilege of paying seven dollars a pouch to a company Google Ventures funded and still couldn't keep alive past 2017. Congratulations: you're the only people who ever got a refund from Silicon Valley and still walked away looking poorer.

facts: Hand-drawn by Chris Costello in 1982 over about six months, when he was 23; he sold the rights to Letraset for $750.
Bundled with macOS and with Microsoft Office, which is why it appears on so many menus and signs.
James Cameron's Avatar (2009) used it for the film's logo and subtitles.
A 2017 Saturday Night Live sketch starring Ryan Gosling is about a man unable to get over that choice.

a.text: Papyrus, you were designed in 1982 by a 23-year-old with calligraphy pens and a dream of ancient Egypt, and somehow you still look like you were drawn by someone shivering. Your edges are so rough you need exfoliating. You promised the wisdom of the Nile and delivered the vibe of a chiropractor's tri-fold brochure. Every day spa, hookah lounge, and "Inner Journey" yoga retreat found you in the dropdown menu and whispered, "This feels ancient." James Cameron spent $237 million on *Avatar* and then used you for the logo, which is like building the Taj Mahal and signing it in crayon. Ryan Gosling lost sleep over you on national television. You're not a typeface; you're a cry for help with ragged little serifs. Even Comic Sans looks at you and says, "At least I know I'm a joke."

b.text:
You opened a day spa. You wanted serenity, mystery, the ancient wisdom of the East. So you opened Microsoft Word and scrolled until something felt like a cucumber on your eyelid. Congratulations: your sanctuary now shares branding with a movie about blue cat people, a sixth-grade report on the Nile, and every church bake sale since 1998. Ryan Gosling lost sleep over James Cameron doing this. You did it for "Serenity Nails & Wax" and slept fine.

And the Mediterranean bistro owner who asked, "How do I show my hummus is authentic?" then picked the font that came free with a Dell. Nothing says "Grandmother's recipe" like your nephew's laptop.

You wanted exotic. You got pre-installed. Nobody relaxes at your spa. They're too busy remembering which school project they typed it on.

facts: Designed by Vincent Connare at Microsoft in 1994, modeled on the comic-book lettering in The Dark Knight Returns and Watchmen.
Made for the speech bubbles of Rover, the cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob; it missed Bob's release and shipped instead in the Windows 95 Plus! pack.
CERN's July 2012 Higgs boson discovery announcement was presented on slides set in it.
The 'Ban Comic Sans' campaign, started by designers Dave and Holly Combs in 1999, ran until 2019, when they retired it and launched usecomicsans.com.

a.text:
Let's talk about the person who posts the boil-water advisory in Comic Sans. You had one job: make residents afraid of their faucets. Instead, E. coli looks like it's coming to a sleepover.

These people think "approachable" is a setting you can click. The office manager typing MANDATORY LAYOFFS in a font Microsoft made for a cartoon dog's speech bubble. Sharon, you're firing forty people in the voice of a golden retriever.

What are they after? Bad news with zero blame. The authority of a memo, the forgiveness of a kindergarten cubby label.

And what does it get them? CERN found the Higgs boson, the particle that gives the universe mass, and announced it in Comic Sans. Humanity's greatest physics breakthrough, and the internet's only question was: who let the dog type?

b.text:
Comic Sans, you were literally designed for a talking dog in Microsoft Bob, and somehow you're the only part of that project that didn't die with dignity. Vincent Connare made you in 1994 for cartoon speech bubbles, and you heard that and thought, "Tombstones. Legal notices. Resignation letters."

Dan Gilbert wrote his furious LeBron James letter in you, and that's why nobody remembers being scared. CERN announced the Higgs boson, the most important physics discovery in fifty years, in you, and the entire scientific community went, "Did a third grader find God?"

People defend you because you help some readers with dyslexia, which is true and lovely, and also the only time you've ever been used responsibly.

You're not a font. You're a bake sale flyer that got tenure. Even Papyrus looks at you and says, "Wow, okay, tone it down."

facts: Released by Bram Moolenaar in November 1991 as 'Vi IMitation', a vi clone he had begun writing for the Amiga in 1988 on top of Stevie; the expansion became 'Vi IMproved' with version 2.0 in December 1993.
Licensed as charityware: the licence asks users to donate to ICCF Holland, a charity Moolenaar ran for children in Uganda.
Stack Overflow's question 'How to exit the Vim editor?' passed one million visits in May 2017, which Stack Overflow marked with a blog post.
Modal editing: in normal mode, typing letters runs commands rather than inserting text; :wq saves and quits, :q! quits and discards changes.

a.text:
Vim, you're the only text editor with its own hostage negotiation thread. Millions of people have viewed the Stack Overflow question on how to leave you. That's not a user base, that's a missing persons report.

You have modes. Normal mode, where typing does nothing normal, and Insert mode, hidden behind the letter "i" like a secret menu.

Your fans move the cursor with h, j, k, l because a terminal from 1976 printed arrows on those keys. That's not efficiency, that's Stockholm syndrome on the home row.

Every Vim user has a 900-line .vimrc copied from a stranger and is too scared to touch it. And when you crash, you leave .swp files behind like a burglar who signs the guestbook.

Even your own kids forked you into Neovim. That's not a fork. That's an intervention.

Goodnight! :wq… :q!… ESC ESC ESC…

b.text:
Let's hear it for the Vim people. You can always spot one, because they'll tell you. Unprompted. Usually while you're mid-sentence about something else, like your divorce.

These folks spent three weekends tuning a .vimrc to save four seconds renaming a variable. That's a payback period of eleven thousand years, but sure, you're the efficient one.

They remapped Caps Lock to Escape and now can't type a password on anyone else's laptop. Their dotfiles repo has more stars than their actual projects. They say "ciw" out loud like it's a spell from a wizard who peaked in 1991.

And what's the prize? You type :wq at the end of every Google Doc. You hit j in Slack and post the letter j to forty coworkers. Congratulations: you're the fastest typist in a room everyone already left.

facts: A rice-noodle dish from Liuzhou, Guangxi; the smell comes from pickled bamboo shoots (酸笋), not from the river snails, which only flavour the broth.
The instant version boomed during the 2020 lockdowns; Liuzhou's government reported packaged luosifen sales of over 10 billion yuan that year.
Added to China's national intangible cultural heritage list in 2021.
Liuzhou opened a luosifen industry college in 2020 to train workers for the trade.

a.text: Luosifen, you're the only dish named after a snail that contains zero snails. They simmer the snails for hours, then throw them out, like a dad who shows up for the paternity test and leaves. Your real star is suan sun, fermented bamboo shoot that smells like a gym sock studied abroad in Liuzhou and came back with opinions. Fans say, "It smells terrible but tastes amazing." So does every scam. You turned instant noodles into a hazmat event: one packet opened in a dorm and three floors file noise complaints, because that smell is *loud*. Couriers wrap you in four bags like evidence. And you come with seven sachets: chili oil, peanuts, tofu skin, wood ear, the bamboo. It's IKEA furniture that makes the neighbors move out. Liuzhou didn't invent a soup. It invented Stockholm syndrome with chili oil.

b.text: You know who you are. You ordered twelve packs off Taobao, waited until every roommate was home, then tore open the sour bamboo shoot sachet like you were declassifying something. You're not hungry. You're making a point. Every slurp comes with the speech: "Smells bad, tastes good." Buddy, we only get the first half. Nobody signed up for the tasting, just the hallway. And you keep saying "it's authentic Liuzhou" like geography is an apology. What does it get you? A spotless pot nobody will borrow, a group chat that goes silent the second you type "anyone want some?", and roommates who suddenly prefer dating people with their own apartments. You came for comfort food. You left with a reputation, a window permanently propped open, and a fridge shelf everyone treats like a crime scene.

facts: Designed by Vincent Connare at Microsoft in 1994, modeled on the comic-book lettering in The Dark Knight Returns and Watchmen.
Made for the speech bubbles of Rover, the cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob; it missed Bob's release and shipped instead in the Windows 95 Plus! pack.
CERN's July 2012 Higgs boson discovery announcement was presented on slides set in it.
The 'Ban Comic Sans' campaign, started by designers Dave and Holly Combs in 1999, ran until 2019, when they retired it and launched usecomicsans.com.

a.text: Let's talk about the people who announce layoffs in Comic Sans. You're not a monster. You're Brenda from Facilities, and you want everyone to feel cozy about the asbestos removal. You took a typeface Microsoft designed for a cartoon dog's speech bubble and used it to type "Your position has been eliminated." That's not softening the blow. That's a clown serving a subpoena. CERN announced the Higgs boson in it, and the physicists who found the God particle spent the week explaining the font. You think it says "approachable." It says "I scrolled right past Arial and Times New Roman and chose a kindergarten birthday invitation." Nobody reads your notice. They screenshot it. Congratulations: your fire evacuation memo is trending, and the building is still on fire.

b.text:
Comic Sans, you were born in 1994 to put words in the mouth of a cartoon dog in Microsoft Bob, and somehow you're the one that survived. Bob is dead. The dog is dead. You're on a sympathy card at a funeral home.

You were inspired by Batman comics, and you've never once been near anything heroic. CERN used you to announce the Higgs boson: humanity's greatest discovery, presented like a lemonade stand. Dan Gilbert used you to call LeBron a traitor, because nothing says "furious billionaire" like bubble letters.

And your defense is always "Well, I help dyslexic readers." Great. You're the guy at the party whose whole personality is a doctor's note.

Even Vincent Connare, the man who made you, says he's barely ever used you. Your own dad won't put you on the fridge.

facts: Published in Warsaw in 1887 by L. L. Zamenhof, a Białystok-born eye doctor, under the pen name Doktoro Esperanto, 'one who hopes'.
Speaker estimates range from 100,000 to two million; roughly a thousand people grow up with it as a native language.
William Shatner starred in Incubus (1966), a horror film shot entirely in Esperanto, with pronunciation Esperantists still mock.
Its Wikipedia has over 350,000 articles, and its Duolingo course for English speakers had 1.36 million learners by July 2018.

a.text: Esperanto learners looked at seven thousand living languages and said, "None of these. I want one with zero places to use it." You wanted to unite humanity, so you picked the one hobby guaranteed to make humanity back away slowly at parties. You signed up to talk to everyone on Earth, and now you talk to a retired Dutch engineer named Joop and a Brazilian guy who keeps sending you poems. Your big payoff is Pasporta Servo, where strangers let you crash on their couch for free, the only time a hobby this niche has ever gotten anyone into a bed. A hundred and thirty years of pushing world peace, and the crowning achievement is still William Shatner's *Incubus*. Zamenhof wanted to end war. You just wanted to be fluent in something before your cousin finishes Duolingo French.

b.text:
Esperanto: the universal language invented in 1887 by a Polish eye doctor who decided humanity needed Italian with a Slavic accent. Universal, as long as your universe is Europe.

The name means "one who hopes." Over a century later: still hoping. There are roughly a thousand native speakers. Klingon is closing in, and Klingon has an army.

It's so logical that "bad" is "malbona," literally un-good. Orwell called; he wants royalties.

Every noun ends in -o and every adjective in -a, so every sentence sounds like a waiter reciting the specials. And it gave us ĉ, ĝ, ŝ and ŭ: letters with little hats, designed for global communication, then made untypeable on every keyboard on Earth.

Its biggest movie starred William Shatner. Even he couldn't oversell it.

facts: Leslie Lamport wrote LaTeX in the early 1980s and released it in 1984 as a macro layer on Donald Knuth's TeX (1978), which Knuth built because he disliked how the galley proofs of the new edition of his own book looked.

TeX's version number converges on π (3.141592653 since 2021), and Knuth's TeX bug bounty started at one hexadecimal dollar, $2.56, doubling yearly until frozen at $327.68; he stopped mailing real cheques in 2008 after fraud and now credits accounts at his fictional Bank of San Serriffe, and only 9 of the 275 cheques he sent from 2006 on were ever cashed.

Its best-known warning is 'Underfull \hbox (badness 10000)'; overfull lines are reported as 'Overfull \hbox (Npt too wide)', and figures float to wherever the algorithm decides, not where the author put them.
A single missing brace can produce an error reported pages away from the mistake, and a document can need three compiler passes to get its references right.

a.text: Let's talk about the guy who writes a two-page memo in LaTeX. Your memo is about the break room fridge, but it's in Computer Modern, so everyone reads it expecting it to end with a theorem. "Fridge Policy, Section 1.1." Buddy, there's no Section 1.2. You spent forty minutes on a preamble longer than the memo. Twelve \usepackage lines to say "label your yogurt." You compiled it three times because the cross-reference said "see Section ??" on page one, referencing page one. You're not after clarity. You're after someone asking, "Is this LaTeX?" so you can say "Oh, habit," like a man who still mentions his thesis at parties. And it gets you exactly one thing: a PDF nobody can edit, so when Karen fixes a typo, she retypes the whole thing in Word.

b.text: LaTeX, you're the only software where "it compiled" counts as an emotional milestone. One missing brace and you blame line 1 of a 400-line file, then sit there with a question mark like we're playing a text adventure from 1985. I put a figure on page 3; you float it to the appendix because you "know better." You have to run twice just to learn your own page numbers, three times if BibTeX shows up, like a guy who needs two friends to remind him his name. Your answer to every problem is another \usepackage, so my preamble is now longer than my thesis. Every paper you touch looks gorgeous, and identical, because everyone on Earth can spot Computer Modern from across a conference hall. And your favorite warning, "Overfull \hbox, badness 10000"? Honestly, that's just how I feel about you.

facts: Created by Rasmus Lerdorf in 1994 as 'Personal Home Page Tools', a set of C programs for tracking visitors to his own résumé page; the name now officially stands for the recursive 'PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor'.
Lerdorf, in his 2007 MySQL Conference talk 'PHP on Hormones': 'I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on.'
Runs WordPress, which W3Techs counted on 39.4% of all websites (58.1% of sites with a known CMS) on 9 November 2026.

Core function names are inconsistent (strpos, str_replace, htmlspecialchars, nl2br) partly because, as Lerdorf confirmed, early function names were chosen to balance a hash table keyed on string length.
Until PHP 8 (2020), the comparison 0 == 'foo' was true because the string was silently converted to a number.

a.text: PHP, you started life as "Personal Home Page," and somehow you now run most of the internet, which explains a lot about the internet. Your own creator said he's "not a real programmer," and honestly, it shows. Is it needle then haystack, or haystack then needle? strpos and in_array have been in a custody battle since 1995. You gave us mysql_escape_string, then mysql_real_escape_string, because apparently the first one was just pretending. Your loose equality swears "0e123" equals "0e456," since both are zero in scientific notation. Your error message for a double colon is T_PAAMAYIM_NEKUDOTAYIM, which is Hebrew, because English wasn't confusing enough. You skipped version 6 entirely, like a kid hiding a report card. Facebook loved you so much they had to rewrite you as a different language. But hey, you power WordPress, so you'll outlive all of us.

b.text: PHP developers are the only people who put a dollar sign in front of every variable and still can't afford rent. You chose a career where "senior" means you remember whether it's needle-haystack or haystack-needle. Your dream job was building the next Facebook; your actual job is the fourteenth WordPress plugin for a dentist in Ohio, deployed via FileZilla. Every conversation you have starts with "PHP 8 is actually really good now," which is what people say about their ex after therapy. You call yourselves Laravel "artisans," because "guy who fixes the contact form" didn't fit on LinkedIn. What does it get you? Job security, because nobody else is willing to open that codebase from 2009 that still calls mysql_real_escape_string. Congratulations: you're unfireable, the way a load-bearing wall is unfireable.

facts: The largest fruit that grows on a tree; single fruits can weigh over 40 kg.
The national fruit of Bangladesh and the state fruit of Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
Unripe flesh is sold as a vegan 'pulled pork' substitute, although it has only 1-2 g of protein per 100 g.
Cutting one releases a sticky white latex, so cooks oil their knives and hands first.
A member of the mulberry family (Moraceae), a relative of breadfruit and figs.

a.text:
Let's hear it for the jackfruit pulled-pork crowd. You found something grandmothers in Kerala have cooked for centuries, slapped "plant-based" on a can, and tripled the price. Bold move, gentrifying a curry.

Your entire pitch is "it shreds like pork." So does a wet paper towel. You know what makes it taste like pulled pork? The barbecue sauce. You're not selling a meat substitute. You're selling a sauce delivery system with a mission statement.

And the protein! Two grams. You told a generation of vegans they're eating a brisket sandwich and handed them a fruit cup in a trench coat.

But hey, it works. You get the Whole Foods endcap, the podcast slot, and the warm glow of saving the planet one eighteen-dollar taco at a time. The pig's still alive. So is your margin.

b.text:
Jackfruit, you're the largest fruit that grows on a tree, which sounds impressive until you realize it just means you're the biggest thing that can fall on someone's head in an orchard. Eighty pounds of spikes dangling at skull height. You're not a fruit, you're a booby trap with seeds.

Opening you requires an oiled knife, rubber gloves, and a tarp, because your sap is basically Elmer's glue with a grudge. Then the smell hits: half Juicy Fruit gum, half onions somebody forgot in a gym bag. You smell like a candy store got food poisoning.

And sure, vegans love you, but only when you're young and taste like absolutely nothing. That's your whole career. The most famous thing about you is that, with enough barbecue sauce, you can pass for a pig. Even your best role is an impression.

facts: Released in October 2012; removed the Start button and booted into a full-screen grid of tiles designed for touch screens most PCs did not have.
The 8.1 update in 2013 put a Start button back, Windows 10 (2015) restored the Start menu, and Microsoft skipped the name Windows 9 altogether.

Microsoft dropped the 'Metro' name in August 2012 after reports that German retailer Metro AG had objected on trademark grounds; Microsoft called 'Metro' a code name and denied any litigation, and the style was afterwards known informally as 'Modern UI'.

a.text:
Windows 8, you looked at a billion people with a mouse and a keyboard and said, "What if your monitor was a giant phone you can't touch?"

You took away the Start button. The one thing a user knew how to find. Microsoft had literally sold Windows 95 with a Rolling Stones song called "Start Me Up," and you said, "Nah."

Want to shut down? Easy: hover in a secret corner, summon the Charms bar, click Settings, click Power. Turning off my computer shouldn't feel like unlocking a cheat code.

Your tiles were so ugly even the name "Metro" had to get dropped over a trademark dispute. Then 8.1 brought back the Start button, which just opened the same tiles. That's not an apology, that's a hostage video.

You were so bad Microsoft skipped the number 9 entirely just to put distance between you and Windows 10.

b.text: You put Windows 8 on a desktop. A tower. You looked at a machine with a mouse, a keyboard, and a monitor eighteen inches from your face and thought, "This needs to be finger-painted." A 2017 genome study in Nature Genetics traced the odour to a duplicated family of MGL genes that pump out volatile sulfur compounds.
China buys most of the world's durian exports, chiefly from Thailand, in a trade worth billions of dollars a year.
Alfred Russel Wallace wrote in 1856 that eating it was 'a new sensation worth a voyage to the East to experience'.

a.text:
Durian, the "King of Fruits." Sure, if the kingdom is a landfill. You're banned on the Singapore subway, right there on the sign next to flammable liquids, because apparently you're the bigger hazard. Hotels fine guests for sneaking you in. That's not a fruit, that's a parole violation.

You wear a medieval mace as a jacket, which is smart, since nobody who's smelled you wants to get close anyway. You fall out of trees and put people in the hospital. You're the only produce that needs a hard hat AND a hazmat suit.

And your fans swear you're "like custard!" Sure: custard aged in a gym bag full of rotten onions. Fifty bucks for a Musang King, and your breath's a crime scene for three days.

Anthony Bourdain ate warthog rectum on camera, and *you're* the one he warned people about.

b.text:
People who eat durian in public aren't hungry. They're recruiting. Every bite comes with a sermon: "You just haven't had a *good* one." Sir, I'm on a bus. I didn't ask to join your church.

Singapore fines people for bringing it on the train, and these folks hear that like a dare. They're the only foodies whose restaurant review gets filed as a police report.

And the payoff? Seventy dollars on a Musang King so you can watch strangers silently change seats. You paid premium to become a fire drill. Your date calls it "an acquired taste," which is exactly what you say about someone you're about to break up with.

Then they stroll back to the hotel, walk right past the sign with a red circle through their entire personality, and still act shocked when housekeeping files a complaint.

facts: Nevada legalized casino gambling in 1931, the year construction of the Hoover Dam began nearby.

a.text:
Las Vegas, the only city where you can see the Eiffel Tower, a pyramid, and Venice in one afternoon and still feel like you never left a strip mall in Ohio. You're a city built in the desert out of pure spite and borrowed water. The Colorado River is literally drying up so a fake volcano can erupt every fifteen minutes for a guy in cargo shorts holding a yard-long margarita.

Your casinos have no clocks and no windows, which is smart, because nobody wants to know it's 9 a.m. on a Tuesday and Grandma's on her third oxygen tank at the Wheel of Fortune slots.

"What happens in Vegas stays in Vegas"? Sure. Mostly your 401(k). And now you've got the Sphere, a giant glowing eyeball, so the whole city can watch you make every mistake in 4K.

b.text: You're not going to Vegas to get rich. You're going to Vegas to donate to a fountain show. Look at you, booking a $49 Spirit flight to "beat the house," like the house didn't build a fake Eiffel Tower with money from guys exactly like you. You've got a roulette "system." You wrote it on a cocktail napkin. Red's due. Red is never due. Red doesn't know you. By midnight you're on Fremont Street feeding a Wheel of Fortune slot in an Ed Hardy shirt you've owned since 2008, telling a stranger you're "only down twelve hundred." By 3 a.m. the Players Club bumps you to Platinum, which is casino for "we'll be needing your kidneys." And you'll call it a win, because they comped you a buffet. Congratulations. You flew 400 miles to pay $3,000 for crab legs.

facts: Spun out in 2013 from the internal chat tool of Tiny Speck's failed game Glitch; founder Stewart Butterfield had earlier spun Flickr out of another failed game.

Salesforce bought it for $27.7 billion in 2021.

a.text:
Slack, you started as the internal chat tool for a failed video game called Glitch, and honestly? Still the most accurate name you've ever had.

You promised to kill email. Instead you gave us email that *knocks*. That little wooden knock-brush sound has triggered more cortisol than any boss in history. I hear it in the shower. I hear it at funerals.

You invented the green dot, so now my employer knows I went to the bathroom for nineteen minutes. You invented "is typing…" so my manager can type for four straight minutes and send "ok."

Threads? Nobody can find them. Huddles? A Zoom call that ambushes you. And somehow every company has 400 channels, and the only active one is #random, where Kevin posts his sourdough.

Your name literally stands for "Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge." Searchable. Sure. Try finding that one link from Tuesday. 👀 reacted by 3 people.

b.text:
Let's hear it for the founders running a company on Slack. You wanted a culture of transparency. You got 340 public channels and every real decision happening in a DM called "quick q."

You don't manage people anymore. You manage a green dot. You jiggle your mouse at your kid's birthday party so the team knows you're "around." Your entire leadership style is the eyes emoji. Someone asks for budget approval, you react with a little thumbs-up, and three weeks later legal wants to know what the thumbs-up meant. Nobody knows. It was legally binding and spiritually ambiguous.

And when something truly matters? You type "hey" and walk away. Just "hey." That's not a message, that's a hostage situation.

You promised Slack would kill meetings. Instead you invented the huddle: a meeting that ambushes people while they're eating.

facts: Descends from Lizzie Magie's The Landlord's Game, patented in 1904 to teach the evils of land monopoly in the spirit of Henry George.

a.text:
Family Monopoly night: for people who looked at Thanksgiving and thought, "This needs more landlords." Dad always grabs the banker job, the only time he's held money he didn't immediately lose. Your sister trades you Baltic Avenue for your Park Place "as a favor," and you realize she's been running the same con since the womb. Mom invented a Free Parking jackpot rule in 1994 and defends it like scripture. And Grandpa just sits in jail, every game, refusing to pay the fifty, finally at peace.

b.text:
Monopoly, you were invented by Lizzie Magie to teach people that landlords ruin lives, and somehow the lesson everyone learned was "buy Park Place." Then Parker Brothers bought you from a guy who basically stole you, which is the most on-brand origin story in history.

You're the only game where "second prize in a beauty contest" counts as income and jail is solved with a coupon. Your mascot looks like he foreclosed on the Pringles guy, and half of America swears he wears a monocle. He doesn't. We just assumed a man that rich would be hiding something.

Nobody has ever finished you. Games don't end; your cousin just flips the board over Marvin Gardens, which you misspelled, by the way. It's Marven. Even your real estate is a scam.

facts: Has been 'about 30 years away' since the 1950s; at the 1955 Geneva atoms-for-peace conference, Homi Bhabha predicted fusion power within two decades.
ITER, agreed in 2006 for first plasma in 2016, re-baselined in 2024 to start research operations in 2034 and deuterium-tritium burning in 2039, at a cost estimated above €20 billion.
NIF's December 2022 'ignition' shot released 3.15 MJ from 2.05 MJ of laser energy; the lasers drew about 300 MJ from the grid to fire.

a.text:
Let's hear it for the fusion people, who have been ten years away since your grandfather was ten years away. These are the only professionals who can miss a deadline for seventy straight years and get a bigger budget every time. Where else does that work? "Sorry, honey, I'll be home for dinner in ten years." "Great, here's twenty billion dollars."

They put the sun in a magnetic donut and act shocked when it won't sit still. ITER's been under construction so long the original welders have grandkids on the crew. And when they finally hit net gain, they celebrated like Moses with the tablets, then mumbled that it doesn't count the electricity for the lasers. That's not net gain. That's me saying I'm up at the casino if you don't count the buy-in.

Ten years, guys. Same as last time. Same tie, too.

b.text:
Nuclear fusion, everybody! The only energy source that's been thirty years away for seventy years. You're not the future, you're a toddler promising to clean his room after the next funding cycle.

You heat plasma to 150 million degrees, ten times hotter than the core of the sun, and still can't do what the sun does for free while being a ball of gas with no PhD.

a.text:
Chicago deep-dish pizza is generally traced to Pizzeria Uno in 1943, though credit is still debated among Ike Sewell, Ric Riccardo, and Rudy Malnati.

The pizza is assembled in an unusual order: cheese first, then toppings, then crushed tomatoes on top. This layering protects the cheese from scorching during the long bake, which is a practical design choice for a pizza that needs considerable cooking time.

Jon Stewart described it as "tomato soup in a bread bowl" and "a casserole." He intended these as criticisms, though one could also view a casserole as a comforting dish.

b.text:
