facts: Created by Rasmus Lerdorf in 1994 as 'Personal Home Page Tools', a set of C programs for tracking visitors to his own résumé page; the name now officially stands for the recursive 'PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor'.
Lerdorf, in his 2007 MySQL Conference talk 'PHP on Hormones': 'I'm not a real programmer. I throw together things until it works then I move on.'
Runs WordPress, which W3Techs counted on 39.4% of all websites (58.1% of sites with a known CMS) on 9 November 2026.

Core function names are inconsistent (strpos, str_replace, htmlspecialchars, nl2br) partly because, as Lerdorf confirmed, early function names were chosen to balance a hash table keyed on string length.
Until PHP 8 (2020), the comparison 0 == 'foo' was true because the string was silently converted to a number.

a.text:
PHP. You started as "Personal Home Page," then rebranded as "PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor," a recursive acronym, because even your name couldn't commit to a stable API.

For twenty years, "abc" == 0 was true, and you called it "type juggling," like a clown proud of dropping things.

strpos takes haystack, needle. array_search takes needle, haystack. That's not argument order; that's mood swings.

Your parse error says T_PAAMAYIM_NEKUDOTAYIM. That's Hebrew for "double colon" and English for "good luck."

You skipped version 6 entirely. Even your release numbers just wanted to move on.

You shipped mysql_real_escape_string, implying the first one was a hoax.

Facebook loved you so much they invented Hack just to avoid touching you.

But sure, you power most of the web. Mostly WordPress. That's like bragging your biggest fan is a raccoon.

b.text: PHP developers are the only people who put a dollar sign in front of every variable and still can't afford rent. You chose a career where "senior" means you remember whether it's needle-haystack or haystack-needle. Your dream job was building the next Facebook; your actual job is the fourteenth WordPress plugin for a dentist in Ohio, deployed via FileZilla. Every conversation you have starts with "PHP 8 is actually really good now," which is what people say about their ex after therapy. You call yourselves Laravel "artisans," because "guy who fixes the contact form" didn't fit on LinkedIn. What does it get you? Job security, because nobody else is willing to open that codebase from 2009 that still calls mysql_real_escape_string. Congratulations: you're unfireable, the way a load-bearing wall is unfireable.

facts: Launched in June 2006 as Google Spreadsheets, built on XL2Web, a product Google acquired from 2Web Technologies.

a.text: You're not running a team. You're running a tab called "MASTER - DO NOT TOUCH," which Brad touched in 2021. Every morning you watch an Anonymous Capybara scroll through payroll and just decide that's fine. Someone sorts column B without selecting column C, and suddenly your top performer is assigned to Linda's maternity leave. Your entire career is "Last edit was 4 minutes ago." You don't do performance reviews, you do Version History. Your conditional formatting has more colors than your company has policies. Your Apps Script was written by an intern who now works at a bakery. Every time someone emails "Request edit access," you feel like a king. And you are a king, ruling over 47 frozen rows and one #REF! that nobody can explain.

b.text: Google Sheets, you're Excel's cousin who got into tech because you could "share a link." Congrats: now forty Anonymous Capybaras can watch me botch a VLOOKUP in real time. Version history isn't a feature; it's a crime scene. IMPORTRANGE says "Loading..." the way my dad said he was going out for milk. You've got a QUERY function that's just SQL in a fake mustache, yet you freeze if I paste more than twelve rows. And #REF! isn't an error message; it's you shrugging in all caps. You cap out at ten million cells. Ten million. You're the only spreadsheet with a bedtime.

facts: Launched by Ty Inc. in 1993 and sold only through small gift shops, with designs 'retired' to manufacture scarcity.

At the height of the craze Beanie Babies accounted for about 10% of eBay's sales, and eBay's 1998 IPO filing said the site at times had over 30,000 Beanie Baby auctions running simultaneously in the quarter ending June 1998.
In 1999 a divorcing couple divided their Beanie Baby collection one by one on a courtroom floor, in a photograph that ran worldwide.
In 1999 Ty announced that Beanie Babies would be retired at the end of the year, then reversed itself after asking the public to vote and seeing an overwhelming vote to keep them.
Most 'rare' Beanies that price guides valued in the thousands now sell for a few dollars.

a.text: Let's hear it for the Beanie Baby investors, the only people who bought a retirement plan at a Hallmark store. You put tag protectors on a heart-shaped piece of cardboard and called it diversification. You drove to four McDonald's for Teenie Beanies, threw away the Happy Meals, and told your kids it was for their college fund. Now that kid is thirty, still paying off loans, and his inheritance is a Rubbermaid tub of Princess the Bears. Every few months you see an eBay listing asking $500,000 for one with a tag typo and think, "Vindicated." Babe, that's not a market. That's another guy in another garage, also lying to his wife. Ty Warner told you which ones were "retired," and you believed him. Ty Warner later pleaded guilty to hiding money offshore. He hoarded too. He just hoarded the right thing.

b.text: Beanie Babies. The only retirement plan where the retiree was a five-dollar bear stuffed with plastic pellets. A whole generation bought plastic protectors for a toy's ear tag, then sealed the toy in a Ziploc so no child could ever love it. You weren't a stuffed animal; you were a 401(k) with a poem on it. And those poems! Ty Warner doing greeting-card Shakespeare for people who thought Princess the bear would pay for college. Princess paid for nothing. Neither did the Teenie Beanies everyone hoarded from McDonald's while throwing away the actual Happy Meal. A divorcing couple in Las Vegas literally split their collection on a courtroom floor, one Beanie at a time. That's your legacy: custody battles over a moose named Chocolate. Even your creator got busted hiding money from the IRS, because he was the only one who ever made any.

facts: Tofu soaked for hours to a day or two in a brine that has itself fermented for months from vegetables such as bamboo shoots and mustard greens, often with dried shrimp or meat; the smell is the brine's, not the bean's.

Changsha's version is black, deep-fried and doused in chili; Taiwan's night-market version is golden and served with pickled cabbage; Shaoxing's, brined with amaranth stalks, is fried pale yellow or steamed with other 'stinky' pickles.
Legend credits Wang Zhihe, a Qing-era exam candidate who left his unsold tofu too long in 1669; a Beijing fermented-bean-curd brand still carries his name.
Street vendors are its main outlet, and the smell carries for a block.

a.text:
Let's talk about the stinky tofu people. You smelled it from three blocks away, a smell like a sewer filed a noise complaint, and your brain said: *that's where we're eating.* Your entire personality is "it tastes better than it smells." That's not a review. That's a hostage statement.

You stand on a Taipei night market curb with a paper boat, chopsticks in one hand, phone in the other, filming your own bravery for followers who can't smell it, which is the only reason they're still following you. Tourists do it once for the story. Locals do it every Tuesday, then board the MRT, where forty strangers silently agree to hate them.

And the pickled cabbage on top? That's you pretending you came for vegetables. You didn't. You came to be the deadliest passenger on the scooter.

b.text: Stinky tofu, you're the only food that announces itself three night-market stalls before you arrive. People don't find you at Shilin. They track you, like bloodhounds following a crime scene. Your whole brand is "smells like a sewer, tastes great," which is also what every bad Tinder date says about himself. You soak for months in fermented brine like you're marinating in a grudge. And your family's no better: Changsha dyed you black, the culinary equivalent of putting sunglasses on a corpse. You need deep frying, chili sauce, AND a mound of pickled cabbage just to be socially acceptable. That's not a garnish, that's a legal team. Your parents gave you one job: be tofu. Tofu's whole personality is having no personality. And somehow you came out smelling like a gym sock that went to college. Honestly? Respect.

facts: Unveiled at Google I/O 2012 with skydivers livestreaming their jump through it onto the Moscone Center roof.
The Explorer Edition sold to invited users in 2013 for $1,500.
Wearers were nicknamed 'Glassholes'; bars, cinemas, and casinos banned the device over its camera.
The consumer programme ended in January 2015; an Enterprise Edition continued until Google stopped selling it in 2023.
Its display was a 640-by-360 prism in the corner of one eye.

a.text: Look at this guy. Paid fifteen hundred dollars to join Google's "Explorer Program," and the only thing he's explored is the sidewalk outside every bar that bounced him. He walks in thinking he's Tony Stark and walks out on a list, because nobody can tell if he's filming, and honestly, neither can he. He's here to meet women, and he gets results: every conversation ends the second he says "OK Glass." Nothing kills the mood like a man asking his own face for directions to her place. He wanted to be the future. Instead the internet had to invent a brand-new word just for him: Glasshole. Silicon Valley promised to connect him to everything. It couldn't connect him to a second date, but it did get him his very own slur.

b.text: Google Glass, you cost fifteen hundred dollars and made everyone wearing you look like a Bluetooth headset that got promoted. Sergey Brin launched you by skydiving onto a building, and that's the last time you were ever cool. You put a tiny prism over one eye so people could check email while pretending to make eye contact. You didn't invent a computer, you invented a reason to get punched. You're the only gadget that gave us a new slur: "Glasshole." Bars banned you. Movie theaters banned you. Robert Scoble wore you in the shower, and that photo did more damage than any privacy lawsuit. You took pictures when people winked, turning every awkward conversation into a potential felony. Your battery died before your reputation did, and that's impressive. Rest in peace: demoted to warehouse work, then quietly killed in 2023. The most Google ending possible.

facts: The largest fruit that grows on a tree; single fruits can weigh over 40 kg.
The national fruit of Bangladesh and the state fruit of Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
Unripe flesh is sold as a vegan 'pulled pork' substitute, although it has only 1-2 g of protein per 100 g.
Cutting one releases a sticky white latex, so cooks oil their knives and hands first.
A member of the mulberry family (Moraceae), a relative of breadfruit and figs.

a.text:
Let's hear it for the jackfruit pulled-pork crowd. You found something grandmothers in Kerala have cooked for centuries, slapped "plant-based" on a can, and tripled the price. Bold move, gentrifying a curry.

Your entire pitch is "it shreds like pork." So does a wet paper towel. You know what makes it taste like pulled pork? The barbecue sauce. You're not selling a meat substitute. You're selling a sauce delivery system with a mission statement.

And the protein! Two grams. You told a generation of vegans they're eating a brisket sandwich and handed them a fruit cup in a trench coat.

But hey, it works. You get the Whole Foods endcap, the podcast slot, and the warm glow of saving the planet one eighteen-dollar taco at a time. The pig's still alive. So is your margin.

b.text:
Jackfruit, look at you. The largest fruit that grows on a tree, and you couldn't even make it to the branches. You just hang off the trunk like a drunk uncle clinging to a lamppost.

You weigh eighty pounds. That's not a fruit, that's a fourth grader in a bumpy green costume. People cut you open and need cooking oil on their hands and knives, because your insides are basically rubber cement. You're the only produce that requires a solvent.

And vegans love you because when you're young, you taste like absolutely nothing. Your big career move is pretending to be pulled pork. Your whole identity is "not bad if you drown me in barbecue sauce."

Then you ripen and smell like Juicy Fruit gum fermenting in a gym bag.

You're the national fruit of Bangladesh, and you still find time to fall on people's heads.

facts: John Sylvan invented the K-Cup in the early 1990s and sold his stake for about $50,000 in 1997; in 2015 he told The Atlantic, 'I feel bad sometimes that I ever did it.'
Keurig 2.0 (2014) read an ink mark on the lid and rejected unlicensed pods; sales fell and workarounds spread online.
By 2014 enough K-Cups were sold each year to circle the Earth more than ten times; the pods were mostly unrecyclable #7 plastic until a switch to polypropylene by 2020.
Keurig Green Mountain merged with Dr Pepper Snapple in 2018 to form Keurig Dr Pepper.

a.text:
Keurig, you took the one drink humanity had perfected over five hundred years and said, "What if it came in a tiny plastic thimble that outlives your grandchildren?" Your own inventor said he regrets making you. When your dad disowns you, that's a phase. When the guy who invented you disowns you, that's a recall.

You make coffee one sad, lukewarm cup at a time, then flash "DESCALE" like a check-engine light for a machine that costs forty bucks. Remember Keurig 2.0? You put DRM on coffee. You were scanning pods like a bouncer: "Sorry, sir, you're not on the list." Nobody was pirating Folgers! And your "Strong" button just drips slower, which isn't strength. That's procrastination.

You're not a coffee maker. You're a plastic-dispensing subscription that occasionally hiccups out hot brown water.

b.text: Keurig people. You wanted coffee but couldn't commit to a whole pot, like a man ordering one buffalo wing. You pay forty dollars a pound for grounds, as long as they arrive in a thimble you throw away. You bought the variety pack, drank every Breakfast Blend in a week, and now there are eleven hot cocoas and a chai you're saving for the apocalypse. You press "Strong" like you're negotiating with it. The guy who invented the pod says he regrets it. You don't. You display your pods on a spinning carousel like fine cigars, and the one time you peeled the foil off to recycle one, you told people about it for a month. You didn't want coffee. You wanted to feel like a hotel guest in your own kitchen. Congratulations: it tastes exactly like that.

facts: Beeple's 'Everydays: The First 5000 Days' sold at Christie's for $69.3 million in March 2021.
OpenSea, the largest NFT marketplace, processed a record $2.7 billion in trades on 1 May 2022 and just $9.34 million on 28 August 2022, a 99% drop, according to DappRadar data.
A 2023 dappGambl study found that 95% of the NFT collections it examined had a market value of zero.
The token usually records only a URL; the image itself sits on an ordinary server or IPFS, not on the blockchain.
Collins Dictionary named 'NFT' its word of the year for 2021.

a.text: Let's hear it for the 2021 NFT buyer. You paid four hundred dollars in gas fees, then made it your Twitter avatar so strangers could right-click save it for free. You joined a Discord with eleven thousand guys named "Chad.eth," called them family, and stayed family right up until the floor price dropped and family started doxxing the dev. You said "WAGMI." We did not all make it. You told your mom you were "early." Early to what? The rug pull? You weren't buying art. You were buying the right to say "few understand" at parties, which was true. Nobody understood, especially you. Jimmy Fallon bought one too. When your financial strategy matches Jimmy Fallon's, that's not a community, that's a support group. The roadmap promised a metaverse. It delivered you, at Thanksgiving, still owing your cousin.

b.text: NFTs, everybody! The only art form where the most common review is "right-click, save." You paid four hundred thousand dollars for a cartoon monkey in a captain's hat, and I have the same monkey as my phone background. The difference? I didn't pay a gas fee bigger than the art. Technically you don't even own the picture. You own a receipt pointing to a link on a server some guy in Ohio forgot to renew. That's not a masterpiece; that's a parking stub for a JPEG. And remember the roadmap? Metaverse, merch, a yacht party! Then the founder pulled the rug, deleted the Discord, and left you holding a "rare trait": sunglasses. Jimmy Fallon showed Paris Hilton his ape on national TV like a proud dad. Now it's worth less than the TV.

facts: Chosen as a compromise because neither Sydney nor Melbourne would accept the other as capital; Australia's constitution required the capital to be at least 100 miles from Sydney.
Designed by the Chicago architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin, who won an international competition in 1912.
Its centrepiece, Lake Burley Griffin, is artificial, created by damming the Molonglo River in 1963-64.
Parliament House (1988) is built into Capital Hill under a lawn meant for citizens to walk over their politicians; the lawn was fenced off in 2017 for security.
Melbourne served as the capital until 1927 while Canberra was being built.

a.text:
You moved to Canberra for the job. Brave. You looked at Sydney rents, did the maths, and decided your personality could be replaced by a security clearance. Now you tell strangers you "can't really talk about what you do," and they're relieved, because it's a briefing note about another briefing note for Senate Estimates.

You came for the ladder: APS5, APS6, EL1, a lanyard that opens one extra door. You stayed because you bought in Gungahlin and the mortgage is now your closest friend.

Every Friday you say you're "basically in Sydney," which means three hours up the Hume, past a giant Merino, to feel alive for one weekend. Then it's back to a Braddon brunch with the same six people from your branch.

But hey, you're close to the snow. You've been once. You'll mention it forever.

b.text:
Canberra exists because Sydney and Melbourne couldn't agree on anything, so they built a city that nobody could possibly be jealous of. Mission accomplished.

It was designed by an American architect, which explains why it feels like a very nice airport with sheep. The roundabouts are so plentiful that locals don't give directions, they give revolutions. The lake is fake, the population is mostly public servants waiting for Friday, and the kangaroos outnumber the nightlife.

Your Parliament House is literally buried in a hill so people can walk on the roof, the only time Australians get to stand on politicians.

For your centenary you commissioned the Skywhale, a giant flying balloon with ten enormous boobs, and somehow that's still the most exciting thing to happen here.

Canberra: home of Summernats, Floriade, and legally purchasable X-rated videos. Burnouts, tulips and porn, because you've got to do something until the next Senate estimates hearing.

facts: Toyota launched the Mirai in 2014; 'mirai' means 'future' in Japanese.
Nearly all US hydrogen filling stations are in California; Shell closed all seven of its California passenger-car stations in February 2024.
More than 95% of the world's hydrogen is made from fossil fuels, mostly by steam-reforming natural gas.
California pump prices reached about $36 per kilogram in 2023-24, over $200 for a Mirai fill; Toyota has handed buyers fuel cards worth $15,000.
Mirai owners filed a class action against Toyota in July 2024 over hydrogen shortages and station outages; a second suit in 2025 sought at least $5.7 billion.

a.text:
Hydrogen fuel-cell cars: the only vehicle where the tailpipe emission is water and the owners are still crying more than the car. The Toyota Mirai loses value faster than a Hindenburg loses altitude. Used ones sell for less than the free fuel card Toyota bundled with them, a card you can't use because the station's been "temporarily offline" since 2022.

You've got a 10,000-PSI tank of the universe's most abundant element, and somehow it's the scarcest thing in California. Filling up costs thirty-six bucks a kilo, and most of that hydrogen is made from natural gas, so congratulations: you bought a gas car with extra steps and a guilt-free bumper sticker.

Hydrogen's been "ten years away" for thirty years. Even fusion's embarrassed for you, and fusion is the same element with better excuses.

b.text: Hydrogen car owners are the only people who looked at Tesla drivers and thought, "Not enough range anxiety." You didn't buy a car; you entered a relationship with the three working pumps in California and an app that tells you which one is "offline" today. You wanted to save the planet. Instead you burned through Toyota's free fuel card in a year at thirty-six bucks a kilo, filling up with hydrogen made from natural gas. Congratulations, you invented a gas car with extra steps. You love saying the only emission is water. Mostly it's your tears at a shuttered Shell station in Fremont. And resale? Your Mirai lost value faster than your friendships after you said "hydrogen economy" at brunch. You're not early adopters. You're unpaid beta testers who drive two hours to refuel.

facts: A Wi-Fi-connected cold-press juicer launched in 2016 at $699, later cut to $399, that squeezed proprietary bags of chopped produce sold by subscription.
Raised about $120 million from investors including Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins.
In April 2017, Bloomberg reporters squeezed the packs by hand and got 7.5 ounces of juice in 90 seconds, faster than the machine's 8 ounces in about two minutes.
Each pack carried a QR code that the press scanned and checked online before squeezing; it refused expired packs and would not run at all unless connected to Wi-Fi.
Shut down in September 2017 and offered refunds on the machine.

a.text:
Juicero, let me say this as plainly as I can, and I think it is worth saying carefully: you were a $699 machine that did the one thing every human hand already does, which is squeeze a bag. Put another way, you were an expensive answer to a question nobody had asked. Bloomberg reporters beat you with their bare fingers: 7.5 ounces in 90 seconds while you wheezed out 8 in about two minutes. To be fair to the reporters, it was not a close contest, and it is hard to imagine a more humbling result for a product of your kind. You lost a race to hardware that comes free with being born.

Honestly, it is difficult to talk about your design without sounding a little incredulous. A juicer that won't run without Wi-Fi. Think about that for a moment, if you can. A bag of chopped produce sat on your tray, waiting for a server to confirm it was allowed to become juice. In other words, the fruit needed permission before anyone could squeeze it. You scanned QR codes like a bouncer at a salad club, checking credentials at the door of a place that serves nothing but vegetables. "Sorry, pal, you're expired." It seems fair to say that this was not the reception anyone hoped for.

Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins gave you about $120 million. That is a sum most companies would consider a generous start, and it is reasonable to expect that it would buy a fairly capable product. You turned it into the world's most expensive stress ball. Even at $399, you couldn't undercut a fist. Your price was reduced, and yet the basic problem remained, which is that a fist was still cheaper and considerably more reliable.

You died in September 2017, offering refunds. Fitting. Finally, something got squeezed out of you.

b.text:
Juicero, you were a $699 machine that did the one thing every human hand already does: squeeze a bag. Bloomberg reporters beat you with their bare fingers: 7.5 ounces in 90 seconds while you wheezed out 8 in about two minutes. You lost a race to hardware that comes free with being born.

A juicer that won't run without Wi-Fi. A bag of chopped produce sat on your tray, waiting for a server to confirm it was allowed to become juice. You scanned QR codes like a bouncer at a salad club. "Sorry, pal, you're expired."

Google Ventures and Kleiner Perkins gave you about $120 million. You turned it into the world's most expensive stress ball. Even at $399, you couldn't undercut a fist.

You died in September 2017, offering refunds. Fitting. Finally, something got squeezed out of you.

facts: Launched in June 2006 as Google Spreadsheets, built on XL2Web, a product Google acquired from 2Web Technologies.
A spreadsheet is capped at 10 million cells (raised from 5 million in 2022).
Functions such as IMPORTHTML, IMPORTXML, and GOOGLEFINANCE pull live web data straight into cells.
Free with a Google account; files live in Google Drive, and collaborators edit the same sheet simultaneously with coloured cursors.

In a browser, offline editing works only in Chrome or Edge, with the Google Docs Offline extension installed and offline access switched on while still connected; the Android and iOS apps work offline natively.

a.text: You're not running a team. You're running a tab called "MASTER - DO NOT TOUCH," which Brad touched in 2021. You wanted a CRM, a project tracker, and an HR system, and you built all three out of IMPORTRANGE and spite. Every morning you watch an Anonymous Capybara scroll through payroll and just decide that's fine. Someone sorts column B without selecting column C, and suddenly your top performer is assigned to Linda's maternity leave. Your entire career is "Last edit was 4 minutes ago." You don't do performance reviews, you do Version History. Your conditional formatting has more colors than your company has policies. Your Apps Script was written by an intern who now works at a bakery. Every time someone emails "Request edit access," you feel like a king. And you are a king, ruling over 47 frozen rows and one #REF! that nobody can explain.

b.text: Google Sheets, you're Excel's little brother who moved into a browser tab and called it "the cloud." Your whole personality is twelve people's colored cursors circling the same cell like sharks while an Anonymous Capybara silently watches everyone's mistakes. You say "Saving..." with the confidence of a man who has absolutely not saved. Your IMPORTRANGE makes me click "Allow access" like I'm asking my own spreadsheet for permission to see my own spreadsheet. Half my cells just say "Loading..." forever, like a Victorian ghost waiting for a letter. And you'll let anyone sort one column without the others, then shrug while every customer gets someone else's phone number. Version history is your only real feature: it's just a timeline of who ruined everything at 2 a.m. And yes, Gemini can explain my #REF! error now. Great. It's still there.

facts: Created by linguist Marc Okrand for Star Trek III (1984), building on a few words the actor James Doohan improvised for the 1979 film.
Deliberately alien grammar: object-verb-subject word order and no verb 'to be', so Hamlet's line became 'taH pagh taHbe'', 'continue or not continue'.
The Klingon Language Institute (1992) published Hamlet 'in the original Klingon'; Bing Translator added Klingon in 2013 and Duolingo in 2018.
Okrand's 1985 Klingon Dictionary listed roughly 1,500 words, and fluent speakers number only in the dozens: 20 to 30 in 2009, 30 to 50 by 2018.

a.text: Congratulations on being fluent in Klingon, a language with maybe thirty fluent speakers, and you've met all of them at the same Marriott. You spent four years mastering a tongue where the standard greeting, nuqneH, means "What do you want?" That's also what your family says when you call. You've read Hamlet "restored to the original Klingon," a phrase only a man who has never been hugged could type. One guy raised his son speaking only Klingon; by age five the kid stopped answering him. That's the dream: a language so pure even toddlers refuse it. There's no word for "please," which explains your dating approach. You learned an entire warrior race's language to tell the barista Qapla'. Success. Sure, buddy. Today is a good day to die... a virgin.

b.text:
Klingon, you're the only language whose native speakers are all fictional and whose fluent speakers all have a Comic-Con badge. Marc Okrand built you in 1984 to sound alien, and he nailed it: you sound like a man choking on a pretzel while reading IKEA instructions.

Your word order is object-verb-subject, so every sentence is a mystery that reveals who did it at the end. Your greeting, nuqneH, literally means "What do you want?" Congratulations: you're the first language designed by a DMV clerk.

You have more apostrophes than vowels deserve, no verb "to be," and a Klingon Language Institute that "restored" Hamlet to its original Klingon. That's not scholarship. That's fan fiction with footnotes.

A linguist once tried raising his son in Klingon. By age five the kid stopped answering. Qapla'!

facts: Released to consumers in January 2007, after the 'Longhorn' project was reset in 2004 and headline features such as the WinFS file system were dropped.
User Account Control prompted so often that Apple's 'Get a Mac' campaign ran an ad about 'Cancel or Allow'.
'Windows Vista Capable' stickers went on PCs that could only run Home Basic, without the Aero interface, and led to a class-action lawsuit.
Windows 7 (2009), widely praised, was largely a tuned-up Vista on the same kernel line; Vista support ended in April 2017.

a.text:
Windows Vista, everybody! Microsoft spent five years building you as "Longhorn," and somehow you still came out premature.

Your slogan was "The Wow Starts Now." You meant "Now" as in "after the loading circle finishes." People bought laptops with "Vista Capable" stickers, which turned out to mean "capable of being sued over." Those machines couldn't even run Aero, so they got a see-through window theme with nothing to see.

And User Account Control! You asked "Are you sure?" so many times that you became the first operating system with separation anxiety.

You came in six editions, including "Ultimate," whose big exclusive was DreamScene: a moving wallpaper for the ten minutes you weren't hunting for printer drivers.

Microsoft had to trick people into liking you. The Mojave Experiment! Your own parents had to put you in disguise.

Your greatest feature? The XP downgrade.

b.text:
Day-one Vista people. You paid $399 for Ultimate Edition because you wanted to be the kind of man whose desktop wallpaper moves. DreamScene. You paid extra for animated wallpaper. Microsoft said "The Wow starts now," and you believed them, lined up at CompUSA at midnight like it was a Harry Potter release.

And what did you get? A computer that asks permission. You'd open a folder and it would dim the whole screen like a disappointed dad: "Cancel or Allow?" You clicked Allow four hundred times a day. Your printer stopped working. Your sound card stopped working. Your Windows Experience Index came back 2.1, and you took that personally.

But you had glass window borders. You had a clock gadget. You had a sticker that said "Vista Capable," which, like you, was technically true and fooled absolutely no one.

facts: Published in Warsaw in 1887 by L. L. Zamenhof, a Białystok-born eye doctor, under the pen name Doktoro Esperanto, 'one who hopes'.
Speaker estimates range from 100,000 to two million; roughly a thousand people grow up with it as a native language.
William Shatner starred in Incubus (1966), a horror film shot entirely in Esperanto, with pronunciation Esperantists still mock.
Its Wikipedia has over 350,000 articles, and its Duolingo course for English speakers had 1.36 million learners by July 2018.

a.text:
Esperanto. In 1887, Dr. Zamenhof, an eye doctor, looked at a world divided by language and decided what it really needed was six letters wearing tiny hats. Nothing says "universal" like ĉ, ĝ, and ŭ, characters no keyboard on Earth can type, so your fans write "cx" and pretend that's fine.

Your name literally means "one who hopes." A hundred and thirty years later: still hoping.

You're the only language where "bad" is just "un-good." *Malbona.* That's not grammar, that's Orwell's Newspeak with a beard. Every noun ends in -o, so you sound like Italian being sight-read by a robot.

You promised world peace and delivered a convention full of men wearing green star pins. Your biggest movie stars William Shatner. And you have about a thousand native speakers, which isn't a language community. It's a cul-de-sac.

b.text: Esperanto learners looked at seven thousand living languages and said, "None of these. I want one with zero places to use it." You wanted to unite humanity, so you picked the one hobby guaranteed to make humanity back away slowly at parties. You signed up to talk to everyone on Earth, and now you talk to a retired Dutch engineer named Joop and a Brazilian guy who keeps sending you poems. Your big payoff is Pasporta Servo, where strangers let you crash on their couch for free, the only time a hobby this niche has ever gotten anyone into a bed. A hundred and thirty years of pushing world peace, and the crowning achievement is still William Shatner's *Incubus*. Zamenhof wanted to end war. You just wanted to be fluent in something before your cousin finishes Duolingo French.

facts: A Portuguese settlement from the 1550s until the handover to China in December 1999.
Casino revenue passed the Las Vegas Strip's in 2006, and at its 2013 peak, about $45 billion, was roughly seven times the Strip's.
One company, STDM, held the casino monopoly for four decades until licences opened to competition in 2002.
Among the most densely populated places on Earth, at roughly 20,000 people per square kilometre.
The Cotai Strip stands on land reclaimed from the sea between the islands of Taipa and Coloane.

a.text:
Macau, you're the only place where the most famous church is just a front wall. Fitting, since the whole city is a facade: a fake Venice with a painted sky, a half-size Eiffel Tower, and a Grand Lisboa that looks like a golden pineapple trying to cheat at baccarat.

Portugal ruled you for 442 years and left behind egg tarts and street signs nobody can pronounce. Four centuries, one pastry.

You've made several times more gambling money than Las Vegas, yet your signature dish is a pork chop jammed in a bun. Classy.

Half your land was dug out of the sea, which is perfect, because the other half was dug out of tourists' pockets.

And they built a 55-kilometer bridge to connect you to Hong Kong, and it's emptier than a junket operator's promises. Even the bridge is losing at the tables.

b.text: You lost it on Hong Kong stocks, so you took the TurboJET to win it back, because nothing says "financial plan" like a ferry with a cancellation policy. You're the guy at the Grand Lisboa squeezing a baccarat card like it owes you rent, blowing on it, peeling the corner so slowly the dealer ages. Red underwear, three days unwashed, "for luck." Baccarat is a coin flip and you've built a religion around it. You told your wife it's a work trip, and technically your work now is the pawn shop next door, which buys Rolexes faster than you can say "one more shoe." By hour nine you're eating an egg tart for dinner and calling it Portuguese culture. You came to win it all back. You leave by bus over the bridge with no luck, no Rolex, and a watch tan.

facts: Written by Brendan Eich at Netscape in ten days in May 1995; named Mocha, then LiveScript, then JavaScript to ride Java's marketing, although the two are unrelated.
typeof null returns 'object', a bug from the first version that has been kept for compatibility ever since.
In March 2016 the author of left-pad, an 11-line npm package, unpublished it and broke builds across the industry, including Babel and React.
[] + {} evaluates to '[object Object]'; {} + [] typed at a console evaluates to 0.
Standardized by Ecma as 'ECMAScript' in 1997 because the name JavaScript is a trademark, first Sun's and now Oracle's.

a.text:
JavaScript, you were built in ten days, and honestly? It shows. You're named after Java the way a knockoff purse is named after Gucci.

You think null is an object. You think NaN is a number. NaN doesn't even equal itself, which makes it the only thing in you with any self-awareness.

Ask you to sort and you hand back, because you alphabetize numbers like a drunk librarian. "11" plus 1 is "111", but "11" minus 1 is 10. Pick a lane.

You needed a second equals sign just to stop lying, and nobody, including you, knows what "this" means.

January is month zero. One guy unpublishing left-pad broke half the internet. And your node_modules folder is heavier than a black hole.

Every week there's a new framework to fix you. That's not a language. That's a renovation.

b.text:
Let's hear it for the people who write everything in JavaScript. You learned one language at a bootcamp and decided the rest of computing could adapt. Backend? Node. Desktop? Electron: a to-do list that eats four gigs of RAM because it ships its own copy of Chrome. Mobile? React Native. Your toaster is probably a Next.js app by now.

You call it "full-stack." Your node_modules folder calls it a landfill. You npm-installed a package to pad a string, and when its author deleted it, half the internet fell over.

Every year you rewrite your whole app in a new framework, then bolt on TypeScript so you can pretend you chose a real language.

And what does it get you? A résumé that says "versatile," and a career spent asking why undefined is not a function.

More than 95% of the world's hydrogen is made from fossil fuels, mostly by steam-reforming natural gas.
California pump prices reached about $36 per kilogram in 2023-24, over $200 for a Mirai fill; Toyota has handed buyers fuel cards worth $15,000.
Mirai owners filed a class action against Toyota in July 2024 over hydrogen shortages and station outages; a second suit in 2025 sought at least $5.7 billion.

a.text:
Hydrogen fuel-cell cars: the only vehicle where the tailpipe emission is water and the owners are still crying more than the car. The Toyota Mirai loses value faster than a Hindenburg loses altitude. Used ones sell for less than the free fuel card Toyota bundled with them, a card you can't use because the station's been "temporarily offline" since 2022.

You've got a 10,000-PSI tank of the universe's most abundant element, and somehow it's the scarcest thing in California. Filling up costs thirty-six bucks a kilo, and most of that hydrogen is made from natural gas, so congratulations: you bought a gas car with extra steps and a guilt-free bumper sticker.

Hydrogen's been "ten years away" for thirty years. Even fusion's embarrassed for you, and fusion is the same element with better excuses.

b.text: Let's talk about the guy who bought a hydrogen car. He wanted to be greener than the Tesla people and smugger than the Prius people, and found the one way to do both while living like a medieval pilgrim. His life is now a map of eleven pumps, and nine say "offline." He loves telling you it "only emits water." Yeah, so does he, every time the app says "station unavailable." He brags that refueling takes five minutes, after the forty-minute drive and the two-hour line behind three other Mirai owners, all quietly weeping. Toyota handed him a fifteen-thousand-dollar fuel card and he burned through it before the warranty paperwork dried. Now he owns a sixty-thousand-dollar car worth a used futon, all to prove he's an early adopter of a future that met him and moved to Japan.

facts: Inaugurated on 21 April 1960 after about 41 months of construction, moving the capital inland from Rio de Janeiro.
Lúcio Costa's Plano Piloto is laid out like an airplane (or a bird, or a cross), with Oscar Niemeyer's government buildings along the fuselage.
Listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987, less than 30 years after it was built.
Planned for 500,000 residents; the Federal District now has about 3 million, most in satellite towns outside the plan.
Built for the car: wide avenues, few pedestrian crossings, and distances that make walking impractical.

a.text: Walking in Brasília is for three kinds of people: architecture students, tourists who trusted Google Maps, and the intern whose ministry is "right next door" on the Esplanada, which here means a forty-minute hike with no shade and a dry-season humidity of 11%. You're not pedestrians, you're pilgrims. You came for Niemeyer and left with heatstroke and a dirt trail you personally wore into the grass, because Lúcio Costa forgot you'd have legs. You cross the Eixão like it's a Frogger level with bureaucrats at 80 km/h, then descend into a tesourinha and come out three superquadras from where you started. Somebody gave you directions: "SQS 308, Bloco C." Congratulations, you're in a spreadsheet. And on Sunday, when they close the Eixão so you can finally walk it, you'll realize there's still nowhere to go.

b.text: Brasília, you're what happens when an architect gets an entire country's budget and nobody says, "Maybe add a sidewalk?" You're shaped like an airplane, which is fitting, because everyone's goal is to board one by Friday afternoon. Your addresses read like Wi-Fi passwords: "SQS 308, Bloco C, apartamento 402." That's not a home. That's a parking spot on a spaceship. Kubitschek promised "fifty years in five," and you delivered: it's been sixty-five years and you still feel unfinished. Your Congress has one bowl facing up to receive the money and one facing down to hide it. You've got a row of identical ministry buildings so nobody can tell which one the scandal came from. In August the humidity drops so low that the only thing drier than the air is a deputy's sense of shame. Even your lake is fake. Honestly? On brand.
